speechtext:
The committee of the cabinet which has been working with the bargaining committees of the unions and of the employers involved in the longshoremen's strike resumed their discussions yesterday afternoon and, as a result, a basis of settlement was agreed upon very early this morning. The minutes of settlement have been drawn up and signed by the bargaining representatives of the parties.
The bargaining committees have agreed to strongly recommend acceptance of the proposals incorporated in the minutes, and these will be laid before the unions represented and the shipping federation not later than tomorrow. If, as I confidently expect, the proposals are accepted, it is hoped and expected that the longshoremen and other workers will return to work in all three St. Lawrence ports on Thursday morning.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, that several of the bargaining agents on both sides are in the gallery. They asked to come to hear the announcement of the settlement.
The fact that such a settlement has come about as a result of hard bargaining between the parties concerned in my opinion justifies

I am sure both parties would want me to express their appreciation to Judge Rene Lippe for the great contribution he has made to the successful outcome of the negotiations.

I think the house and the Canadian public generally would be interested to know that some of the difficulties in this case have arisen out of the technological and other changes in the stevedoring industry which have taken place during recent years. The workmen felt they were entitled to substantial increases in remuneration for their services, and the employers were prepared to agree to substantial increases in return for an assurance of greater productivity in line with the changes to which I have referred.
It was difficult if not impossible for the parties to agree on the nature and extent of possible increases of productivity. When this situation developed I, as Minister of Labour, several weeks ago announced that I intended to set up a commission of inquiry under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act to inquire into the possibilities of improving productivity, yet at the same time ensuring job security for any members of the unions concerned who might be directly affected by new methods of operation and technological changes.
I now wish to confirm that I intend to set up such a commission within the next few days. I will have more to say on that subject when I announce the appointment of the commissioner.

Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the house appreciate how
(Mr. Nicholson.]
these negotiations can drag on without intervention by the government in a collective bargaining process, crippling the economy and harming the country. Consequently the announcement we heard last night that the strike had been settled pleased us just as much as it must have pleased the government. We hope the settlement arrived at after negotiation is satisfactory to both parties, and we are pleased that the agreement has now been ratified.
Let me point out that this was not an ordinary situation, but a situation that dragged on from November of 1965, when a breakdown in negotiations between the two parties took place. The government sat around hoping this situation would go away and that some miracle would be performed by someone other than themselves to bring about the settlement that was so vital to the economy of our country.
On May 9, 1966 the longshoremen walk-out was called illegal by the employers, and it was not until May 24, 1966 that it was considered to be legal; yet during all that time the government sat around waiting and hoping, in spite of the urgings on this side of the house in a serious vein, that it would somehow settle itself. It was not until last night that the advice we put forward was accepted by the government.

subtopic: QUEBEC-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SETTLEMENT OF LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there will be a sigh of relief across this country that the longshoremen's strike has now ended. I can assure the Minister of Labour and the Prime Minister that the members of this party are very happy that a solution has been found without the necessity of parliamentary intervention. Perhaps the proposal we made last week for
June 14, 1966

parliamentary intervention without compulsory arbitration may have had some bearing on bringing the parties together. This house and the country ought to express appreciation to Judge Lippe and the Minister of Labour, both of whom worked very hard in search of a solution.
I hope we will receive from the minister very soon some details as to the terms of the settlement. The minister mentioned, for instance, that he is going to set up a commission of inquiry to look into the question of the reduction of work gangs. While the minister uses the term "productivity", I take it from the statements made by the shipping federation that when they refer to productivity they are talking about getting the same amount of work done with smaller work gangs.
I certainly have no objection to the idea of setting up a commission of inquiry to look into this matter, providing the decisions and recommendations of that commission are not binding upon both parties but are simply for the purpose of providing a basis upon which collective bargaining negotiations may continue. I hope the minister will give us some more information about that, perhaps when the orders of the day are called.
The government are very happy at the outcome, as we all are; but may I suggest to the government that they need not be too happy. This strike has been a costly affair; it has cost this country millions of dollars, and there must be some lessons which can be drawn from it. One of the lessons is that our methods of conciliation are outmoded, that we are appointing mediators only days before a strike deadline is upon us. We have now been negotiating the longshoremen's strike on the basis of an agreement which was supposed to commence on January 1 last. Surely with the rash of labour disputes which are now before us we cannot have the cabinet sitting up half the night for several days in order to settle each of these disputes. There must be some better way and some more up to date method of conciliating these labour disputes.
I suggest to the government that this strike ought to convey to them the fact that there are deep underlying causes not only for this strike but for the other strikes that are threatened in Canada. The two underlying causes are first, the increasing cost of living which gives rise to a demand for increased
Labour Relations
wages. We will continue to have labour disputes and labour discontent until the government grapples with this problem of the spiralling cost of living. The second of the basic causes of this strike, as of other strikes, has to do with the effects of automation or, as the shipping federation have called it, increased productivity. Increased productivity and automation inevitably mean the displacement of men. Unless the government are prepared to set up the necessary machinery whereby the men who are displaced, if they are young enough are retrained or if they are old enough are retired on a pension to which the employer will make the major contribution, we will continue to have labour disputes.
We in this party believe that the benefits of technology do not belong exclusively to management and that the workers, especially the workers who are displaced by automation, have a right to some of the benefits or the savings through technology. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, while we are delighted that this strike has now been ended, in view of the prospect of many other labour disputes and probably some other strikes we hope the government will now begin to tackle the root causes, rather than always picking up the pieces of the crises which they have so long neglected.

Now, we are faced with another prospective strike, because a strike by the workers of the seaway is being announced for Friday of this week. Why does the government not take position now and intervene at this point, before the employees of the seaway go out on strike which is scheduled for Friday, just as the Prime Minister did last night for the longshoremen's strike?
Mr. Speaker, the workers need security. A while ago the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) was saying that automation is becoming a grievous problem which will bring about more strikes eventually in any province of Canada.
There is a solution to those strikes, which are disastrous not only for the Canadian people, but for the strikers themselves, because they lose thousands of dollars.
Mr. Speaker, the solution the government should consider would be to meet with management and the unions, so as to discuss with both parties the possibility of enabling, for instance, the workers to share in the profits of the undertaking. This would be the ideal solution: when a person is a partner in an undertaking, he feels more responsible. This solution would prevent disastrous strikes for the Canadian people in general.
In order to prevent strikes I suggest that the government should urge management and labour leaders to consider jointly the advisability of allowing all employees, all workers, the entire Canadian labour force to share in the profits of business concerns.
Then Canada would grow, Canadian productivity would increase and the administration of the country's business would be spared a great deal of trouble.

Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that much satisfaction has been expressed by the Minister of Labour on the settlement of this very serious strike which has had far reaching national implications. It is equally obvious that there are many who would like to share in the credit for the settlement. Whether we believe the government should have taken more initiative earlier, and whether the negotiations could have been shortened, we are glad that an agreement has been reached to the satisfaction of both employers and employees, as well as to the relief of the people of Canada.
Perhaps we should draw attention to the fact that we are already on the threshold of
[Mr. Caouette.l
another strike, that of Air Canada employees. We are also faced with threatened strikes of the seaway workers, the C.N.R. employees and the international woodworkers on the west coast. It is obvious that foresight and advance planning are needed to help labour and management cope with the new problems which are raised by automation and by the continuing increase in the cost of living.
In this regard it is gratifying for those workers who were involved in this strike that some measure of justice has been brought to help them meet the increase in the cost of living, but there are literally hundreds of thousands of people living on fixed incomes, in particular pensioners whose pensions were set on a cost of living lower than it is now and who cannot resort to a strike. We see this problem in its proper perspective when we realize that it affects all Canadians, not only those involved in the strike action or the threatened strike action.
I believe the government must take the lead to assist labour and management in such matters as retraining, job security and unemployment. Manpower mobility assistance is not enough. If we wait until management is forced to instal new processes to increase productivity and enable it to compete for markets, then labour has no choice but to exert pressure to protect its workers. It is therefore imperative that joint labour-management-government committees be set up to study these problems before they are upon us. I believe it is now necessary, as we express our gratitude for what was done last night and this morning, to move forward and deal with those strikes which face us now.
I wish to add, Mr. Speaker, that we join in the expression of appreciation for what has been accomplished. We also wish to voice our appreciation to Judge Lippe together with the members of both negotiating parties for the final agreement.

speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the establishment of a health resources fund to assist provinces in the acquisition, construction and renovation of health training facilities and research institutions and for the appropriation in conection therewith of the sum of five hundred million dollars to be credited to the fund in such amounts as from time to time are required and to provide for contributions therefrom to the provinces; to provide further for the establishment of a health resources advisory committee consisting of eleven members and for the payment of reasonable travelling expenses of its members.
Motion agreed to and the house went into
committee, Mr. Batten in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR HEALTH TRAINING AND RESEARCH FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am
pleased to begin the discussion on this resolution setting up a health resources fund. As hon. members are aware, the government proposes to introduce shortly legislation under which it will be possible to give financial support to the provinces for the provision of medical care benefits. Such a program will undoubtedly help to create a professional climate which will attract increasing numbers of able people to the study and practice of medicine and related professions and will thereby improve still further the quality of care available to our people.
Health Resources Fund
We are well aware that this would involve large investments in training and research facilities. Furthermore, the strengthening of such resources requires time, and planning must be initiated at an early date. It was in this context that the Prime Minister announced last July the proposal of the government to establish a health resources fund. At the same time, the Prime Minister promised that the terms of reference for the fund would be developed only after consultation with provincial governments through a conference of ministers of health which he proposed should meet at an early date.
In September, therefore, a federal-provincial conference of ministers of health was convened in Ottawa. Prior to this meeting departmental officials had visited the provinces to confer with their counterparts in order to acquire some of the necessary background data to assist the government in giving consideration to the appropriate size of a health resources fund. When the provincial ministers of health met, therefore, the Prime Minister was able to announce in more specific terms governmental proposals with regard to the size of the fund. At that time he announced that the government proposed to establish a fund in the amount of $500 million to be available over a 15-year period. The basic purpose of the fund is to help meet the greater need for trained people to provide medical care services and to endeavour to catch up where possible in areas where adequately trained personnel are in short supply. The moneys to be made available through the health resources fund will support the construction and equipment of facilities for health research and training. Capital grants will be available for the construction, renovation and basic equipment for research establishments, teaching hospitals, medical schools, as W'ell as training facilities for essential health personnel. It is not proposed that the funds provided through this program will be available to meet the operating costs of such establishments.
At the September meeting of the ministers of health it was agreed that since it is the provincial governments which are responsible for the types of facilities which will benefit from the fund, the allocation of the fund moneys obviously would require a considerable degree of consultation with the provinces. In conformity with this view it was decided to appoint an ad hoc technical committee

June 14, 1966
Health Resources Fund charged with the task of establishing estimates of immediate and foreseeable needs for health and research establishments, medical schools, teaching hospitals, schools of dentistry, schools of nursing, and training facilities for other health personnel. In the light of these estimates the committee was requested to make proposals for the general regional distribution which might govern the allocation of funds through provincial governments. This committee was also requested to make proposals for the method of allocating funds having regard to a desirable degree of consultation.
The ad hoc committee which met in October consisted of a representative from each of the provincial governments as well as representatives from the Medical Research Council and several of the large national professional associations representing doctors, dentists, nurses and hospitals. The committee submitted to the conference of ministers a report which I tabled in this house on February 2, 1966.
The conference of ministers had by this date completed its consideration of the report. It had dealt with proposals relating to preliminary estimates of provincial needs, the need for long-range projections, principles recommended for identifying certain type of facilities, the basis for allocation of funds, and the establishment of a health resources advisory committee for which were set out suggestions concerning composition and functions.
e (3:40 p.m.)
The conference of ministers accepted for the most part the proposals set out by the technical committee in its report although the proposal relating to the composition of the advisory committee was not supported by the ministers of health. The ministers suggested that such an advisory body should consist of representatives of the federal and provincial ministers of health and they recommended that the committee call upon professional bodies for advice on technical matters.
It was agreed that requests for assistance from the health resources fund would emanate from provincial governments in whose field of jurisdiction matters of health reside.
It will be noted that throughout the planning of the health resources fund the federal government has stressed the importance of close consultation and continuing liaison between the federal and provincial governments at all levels. Over the years the department

has maintained the closest possible relationship of this sort with the provincial departments to the mutual benefit of all concerned, I should like to take this occasion to express a word of public appreciation to provincial health authorities who at all levels have always worked very closely with my departmental officers.
Although planning has been carried out over many months in connection with the health resources fund, there are still many details to be worked out. As soon as the necessary legislation has been passed by the house the advisory committee authorized by this resolution will be established, and it is my hope that it will be possible to convene a meeting of this body as expeditiously as possible.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, I should like to repeat the words of the Prime Minister when he first announced the intention of the government to launch this program. He said that what is now under consideration is among the most important investments in the human resources of Canada that have ever been planned. While there will be many difficulties to overcome and much careful preparation will be needed, he expressed confidence that the federal and provincial governments could go forward in this matter with a high sense of common purpose.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to congratulate the minister for introducing the health resources fund measure but I can only say that in my opinion it is far too little and too late to cope with the future plans upon which the minister will be embarking. Those plans will require an increase in personnel to look after the health of the people of Canada. We shall require more doctors and more technicians, radiologists, physiotherapists, nurses, dentists and psychiatrists.
A sum of $500 million is to be set aside for this fund, but as far back as October, 1964, Mr. Robarts, the premier of Ontario, said that his province was launching a $114 million blitz program to train doctors, nurses and dentists. Further, in a report in the Toronto Star J. T. Allen has indicated that 70 to 75 doctors per year will be trained in a new medical science centre and that this will require an expenditure of $500,000 per year per doctor and for 500 first year doctors this will mean that a total sum of $250 million per year will be expended.
This is a matter of simple mathematics. Although $500 million sounds like a lot of
June 14, 1966

money the Hall commission report states that we must graduate 500 new doctors per year. Four new medical schools must be built by 1970 but it must be remembered that to start with we shall need 500 new doctors per year. Ontario is expecting Ottawa to pay a third of the cost per student which would mean a total of $46 million instead of the $33 million that has been mentioned.
I understand that Ontario alone will need $75 million for university capital costs. Given all these figures I want to say to the minister that if there is any part of education that can be made universal and national it is medical education. Every doctor graduating from a medical school takes the Canadian Medical Council examinations. The standard is uniform and therefore the minister need not worry about stepping into a national medical education policy. It is already there.
I would like to ask the minister whether under the provisions of the health resources fund there is any remuneration incentive for graduates. Last year close to 800 doctors crossed the Canadian border into the United States. To train each of them required a minimum of $25,000. If each stays in the United States he will earn approximately $500,000 during his lifetime, and 800 times $500,000 amounts to $400 million. There is an annual loss to Canada of $400 million, which shows the insufficiency of this $500 million health resources fund. The same is true of other professions.
I would also like to ask the minister whether anything is being done to increase incentives for doctors who stay in Canada. Taxation is a federal matter. Has the minister considered tax incentives for students after graduating and for postgraduates which will tend to keep them in Canada rather than lose them to the United States at a cost to Canada of $400 million per year?
At present there is a great shortage of physiotherapists and other technicians. By July my own hospital will be down to two technicians although we need five. We hope to import two from the Philippines but we will still be short.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Last year federal funds covered just 40 per cent of our research projects. How then can this $500 million be stretched to cover all the things we need? If there is one thing that will keep good teachers and people interested in research in Canada it is fine research centres. Without proper facilities we cannot
Health Resources Fund keep these people here and without the research itself we will not develop the doctors and trained personnel we need.
In 1958 the Conservative government doubled the per capita hospital grant. The minister will say we are continuing these grants for the next two years but I wonder whether he realizes that costs have gone up and up and up. I believe that costs per bed were around $6,000 but today they are around $20,000. In 1958 we doubled the grant from $1,000 to $2,000. In addition we gave $750 per bed for nurses and internes' quarters, radiologists' rooms and so on. But here we are in this parliament in 1966 not doing one solitary thing to remedy the situation. Here we are doing the same old thing we did in 1958. Yet we have accepted one-third, or one-half if you wish to put it that way, of the responsibility for hospitalization for the people across Canada. I should like to ask the minister why the federal government has not accepted a third of the cost shared with the provinces and the municipalities. In construction costs the municipalities are now holding the bag with the provinces. If I remember the statistics correctly, last year the federal government paid exactly 12 per cent of capital construction. This is not good enough when we consider municipal taxes, the cost of living and all the other things that weigh heavily on the municipalities. Yet they are asked to carry a disproportionate load.
The health resources fund is a good thing but I do not think it is half enough. We lose $400 million through doctors going to the United States but the government still comes up with a fund of only $500 million. This does not make sense to me. I should like the minister to take a good look at the problem to see whether or not the grants should be increased and whether they should accept one-third of the cost of construction. Several times when this matter has been mentioned to me I have felt like shrinking down and getting out of sight when I see the federal government asking the municipalities to carry the load which we should be carrying here. Mr. Chairman, I will have other questions to ask at a later time.

Mr. Chairman, we in this party welcome the advent of the health resources fund, at least in its resolution form. However, like the hon. member who has just spoken I am afraid it is going to be much too little too late. An aircraft crashed last week in California and its value

June 14, 1966
Health Resources Fund alone was $500 million. So it looks as it we are placing our health resources fund at a level equal to the value of one aircraft.
I should like to limit my remarks to the medical situation. In the Hall commission publication, "Medical Manpower in Canada", Judek shows that our medical manpower is inadequate and that in the ratio of population to physician we compare unfavourably with such countries as the United States, Germany and Italy. He estimates that as of 1961, 3,900 more doctors would have been needed in private practice to fulfil unmet demands for medical services. We can be sure that the gap has widened since.
Even if we leave the possibility of medicare aside, and we seem little closer to it now than we were 45 years ago, our requirement for medical personnel will increase sharply. Our population is growing fast and by 1990 can be expected to be over 35 million. Within our population there is a greater awareness of and demand for medical treatment. At the same time, old diseases are succumbing to research while new diseases appear.
Strong and immediate action is necessary to fulfil the needs of the present and to prepare for the future. This situation, like Gaul, resolves itself into three parts. We must solve the problems of schools, teaching facilities, teaching staff and, perhaps most of all, of students themselves.
In the field of construction and equipment for teaching facilities we welcomed the announcement in July of a $500 million fund to cover such expenses. We are glad now that something is being done. It is interesting to note that if Ontario carries out its proposed $300 million construction expenditures in the next seven years, with the federal government paying the recommended 50 per cent, it will run out of its share of the fund quite early in the program. We hope that the government will make provision for a periodic review of the sums available so that they may be increased.
In the field of nursing the Hall commission has demonstrated our acute shortage of personnel. It has recommended the expansion of existing university schools of nursing and the establishment of at least ten more in the next four years. At least 50 per cent of these construction and equipment costs should be borne by the federal government.
To cover our shortage of dentists the Hall commission calls for the expansion of our five existing dental schools and the construction of five new schools in the next ten years.

Here again, 50 per cent of the cost must be the responsibility of the federal government. To keep up with medical education we must expand and improve our existing schools and build seven more in the next ten years. For these and for associated teaching hospitals the federal government should pay 50 per cent.
In the field of medical research the Far-quharson committee of 1959 stressed the urgent need for research buildings and facilities and estimated that $25 million would be needed from the federal government. The Hall commission publication, "Medical Education in Canada", has repeated the recommendation. While medical research is of enormous importance in itself, it has an important bearing on medical and dental education. Almost all university medical teachers engage in research, and for most of them this is their chief interest. If research funds are not readily available, we will not be able to attract good teachers nor keep them when we get them.
In the 1964 report of the Medical Research Council Dr. Ray Farquharson wrote as follows:
The most important investment in medical science is to educate students well, and to train gifted young graduates in the art and practice of research. This can only be accomplished when the teachers themselves understand medical science and have practised it. Many more teacher-scientists are needed now, both because of the expansion of our medical schools and because of the rapid growth of medical science. Some of these teachers will not continue to carry out intensive medical research, but all should have a research approach to their teaching if they are to give their students the necessary instruction and practice in critical thinking and in the evaluation of evidence . . . Without . . . active research, covering a very wide range, the care of patients sick with related disorders would certainly suffer.
He pointed out the lack of funds for salaries for teachers and scientists and the lack of funds for facilities. He went on to say:
The loss of our competent medical scientists to the United States would be greatly reduced if we had the funds needed to support them personally, and if the facilities necessary for their work were provided in Canada.
The Hall commission has recommended that the Medical Research Council be changed into an independent health services research council and that funds available to it should be increased by $2 million per year. The Bladen commission of 1965 went even farther. It recommended a grant to the Medical Research Council of $20 million in 1966-67,
June 14, 1966

with a 20 per cent increase each year thereafter. It recommended further that research grants to universities should carry an unconditional 30 per cent supplement to the university concerned, to come from the fund just mentioned.
A new report, prepared for the Canadian Society for Clinical Investigation and presented to the Prime Minister early this year, has called our present level of medical research inadequate. They have said that the federal government must become the chief source of expanded funds and they estimate that at least $140 million will be required before 1970 to build and equip facilities for an appropriate standard of research. They say:
Unless support to medical research is provided at the suggested levels as rapidly as possible, a deterioration in the standards ot Canadian medical schools and in the quality of health care provided to the Canadian people is in prospect.
They conclude the report thus:
-it is imperative that a research environment be established which will encourage individuals to enter medical science as a career, which will induce leading teacher-scientists to stay in Canada, and which will attract back to Canada those who have gone elsewhere for lack of opportunity in their own country.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
It is interesting to note that this report has been endorsed by the deans of our 12 medical schools, by voluntary health organizations and by hundreds of Canadian medical scientists. Certainly a greater responsibility for research on the part of the federal government will be necessary to develop and maintain good medical teachers.
In nursing it has been found that 75 per cent of hospital instructors and 56 per cent of university instructors are not even minimally qualified. When one considers the salaries paid one can only be surprised that so many are qualified.
To bring the present situation to proper standards and to provide for future needs the Hall commission recommended that the federal government contribute to greatly increased salaries for these teachers comparable with salaries in similar fields.
In medical and dental teaching qualification is not now a problem but salaries are a continuing deterrent to teaching as a career. The average income of a doctor engaged in research is less than half that of his colleague in private practice. In order to provide the medical teachers we need we must make
Health Resources Fund available many more postgraduate opportunities simply to train teachers in the increasingly complex and diversified fields of medicine. Research funds and operating funds must be greatly increased to attract and to hold competent people within our educational structure, and in this the federal government must carry its share of the load.
We come now to the problem of the students themselves. No educational system will work if it fails to attract students and there has been a distressing decline in the number and quality of young people seeking education in the health sciences.
In order to attract more nursing students we must first consider their financial position. Student nurses earn little or no money and those without financial help cannot consider training. The Hall commission has recommended that assistance be provided for student nurses in the same manner as for other hospital students. It has also been recommended that hospital nursing courses be shortened to two years, eliminating much of the free labour which nurses exchange for their training. This would increase the operating costs of teaching hospitals but we can ill afford to continue using trained nurses to do char work.
For medical students availability of money is of paramount importance. The medical course is the most expensive in any university and the one, paradoxically, where the fewest scholarships are available. In the 1961-62 school year the average student expenditure was $2,250. Of the few scholarships and bursaries available the median value was $325.
The Hall commission has recommended scholarships of $2,000 a year in the last two years of the course, depending only on satisfactory progress. We must also make arrangements whereby the cost of postgraduate training is at least income tax deductible, if not directly subsidized. Once a medical student has completed his degree he still has a period of poverty before him as an interne and resident. In 1960 the average income of an interne was $1,740 and for a resident, $3,360. This obviously constitutes a barrier in the recruitment of students and salaries must be raised to provide proper compensation for these doctors.
During the post-war years total university enrolment in the 20-24 year age group rose from 7.1 per cent to 8.9 per cent. Medical student enrolment during the same period fell from 3.5 per cent to 3.2 per cent.

I have also noted that this resolution deals with research institutions, and I think that in the past we have largely failed in that respect and we still have much to do in the future to prevent illness and contagious diseases, or at least to control an outbreak. I think that those research institutions can be quite beneficial to the Canadian public and will meet an ever increasing need in countries with a similar standard of living.
Mr. Chairman, on the whole I think that this resolution deserves all the attention of

hon. members and we are impatiently awaiting the bill which will give us the very essence of the proposed resolution; at that time, we will take a greater part in the consideration of this bill, item by item, and we shall have other remarks to make at that time.

In this way all the courses are going to be brought together in an over-all program covering the medical services that are required and must be provided for the Canadian people.

June 14, 1966
Health Resources Fund
Reference has been made to the ad hoc committee which was set up to study this particular matter and to several of the terms of reference of that committee, such as the question of regional distribution of funds and several other matters. Mr. Chairman, the resolution before us asks the house to approve a fund which will help to finance health training facilities and medical research institutions. As a member from Montreal this proposal has great interest for me and for the people of Montreal. Montreal has long been known as one of the great medical centres of the world. Among its great training and research hospitals are the Royal Victoria Hospital, the Montreal General, the Montreal Neurological Institute and many others. There are also extensive research facilities at McGill University, the University of Montreal and many nursing schools.

[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I mention these things, Mr. Chairman, not to promote my own city but to remind all hon. members of the national medical institutions which are located in Montreal. I use the word "national" because these institutions, in contrast to other hospitals and research centres, serve the medical needs of all Canada and not merely of the inhabitants of the Montreal area. There is no doubt that there are several other national medical centres in Canada about which similar comments could be made.
It is because of the national function of such institutions that the government has seen fit to set up this fund. Medical science and technology have developed to such an extent that they can no longer be carried on by small privately financed teams. It is not even possible for the required facilities to be provided by provincial financing. As other hon. members have said, many of our provinces are too small to provide the large resources necessary to give their people the proper medical personnel and research. In a country of barely 20 million people it is essential that such facilities be shared and financed on a national basis.
A further reason for setting up such a fund is to provide capital in Canada for the most up-to-date research facilities. In an age when change takes place so quickly and discoveries are soon outdated after they are put in production, it is necessary that finances be made available to keep pace with these changes. Although Canada is presently producing many fine young doctors and research scientists, a good number of them are obliged to leave the country to find facilities and programs which will allow them to do advance research and study. If we are to keep these highly trained citizens, then we must give them the opportunity to work here in Canada.
It is to be noted that this resolution has been mentioned in conjunction with the proposed medicare bill and the proposed Canada Assistance Plan. It is obvious that if we are to establish a plan to provide medical care to all Canadians we will have to provide hospitals and personnel to give this care. Some Canadians have argued that the shortage of hospitals and medical personnel are foremost reasons for not introducing medicare. This is not valid. If we were to follow that reasoning we would still have a system where health depended on wealth and where many would go without proper medical care.
June 14, 1966

We need a system of medicare; we also need the development of health resources. The members of any modern society are interdependent. The economic, social and political well-being of any citizen will depend to a great extent on the good health, education and industriousness of his neighbours. If a large segment of the society is in poor health, this will affect the whole society. I remember a few years ago when we had the Asian flu epidemic and I was shocked to learn of the large scale economic loss to the country due to absenteeism and other side effects which resulted from it.
I hope, Mr. Chairman, that this initiative of the federal government will be followed by a greater effort on the part of corporations and individuals who can also do much to help in this area. No matter how great the contribution of the government there will always be a need for private action.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I would like to refer briefly to a subject which was mentioned by other hon. members, the situation with regard to nurses. I do not think that any other group, trained professionally for many years, is treated so poorly. There is no doubt that these young women perform a great service for Canada and it is unfortunate that they are often not paid as well as those who are far less deserving. I hope that this plan will also provide assistance to preventive medicine and mental illness. In all, I think this resolution is a commendable one and deserves our full support.

Health Resources Fund envisaged will come to a total of $514,250,000. I was assured by the Association of Canadian Medical Colleges that at present this figure would be much higher because of the increase in current costs.

Some mention has been made of the ratio of doctors to the population of Canada. There are 20 countries in the world which have a more favourable ratio of doctors to the population. We do know that a very large number of our physicians are overworked and do not have time to keep up to date with medical progress. In order to take care of our present needs and to maintain the present ratio, which is one doctor for every 859 Canadians, we must register 1,300 new physicians every year. At present our medical schools produce 850 physicians a year. I think it is very significant that were it not for the fact that we enjoy the immigration of 400 to 600 physicians from countries all over the world we would be in a very serious position indeed. As a matter of fact, the immigration of doctors could very well be reduced significantly. As we know, there is a serious shortage of doctors in Great Britain and attempts are being made to persuade them to stay there instead of emigrating to other countries.
We in Canada have received many very well trained physicians from the Philippines, but the government of the Philippines is attempting to refuse, and I think succeeding, permission to doctors to emigrate from that country because of their own great need of physicians. What about the other side of the question? What about those who are leaving the country? I believe there is a significant report in the Gazette of January 20, 1966, in which Dr. Barrie Pierce, who is about 40 years old and a Canadian professor at the University of Michigan, makes these statements:
-the brain drain of top-flight medical and scientific men is growing worse and presents a great threat to the country. If you think you have a problem in medical education today, you can rest assured it will become worse. Competition for these high quality men is increasing all the time, especially in the United States where a drastic expansion will take place in the coming years.

June 14, 1966
Health Resources Fund
He pointed out that the United States is
importing some 1,500 physicians per year and Canada is one of the main sources of supply.
The minister said, and he seemed to state this unequivocally, that the health resources fund would result in improved medical care and the attraction of people to the medical profession. I wish that were true. I could point out to him the situation in Saskatchewan. The University of Saskatchewan established a medical school for the definite purpose of trying to obtain more physicians for Saskatchewan. The major purpose was to increase the doctor supply in our province. The results of this program were studied carefully by Dr. Samuel Wolfe, whose name will be familiar to the members of the New Democratic Party, I am sure. His report in the Canadian Medical Journal of a year ago contains a detailed analysis of this matter and demonstrates that as a result of setting up our medical school we have 40 per cent fewer Canadian graduates practising in Saskatchewan today than there were before. I heard the minister say that immediately following the passage of this resolution and the bill based upon it the government would introduce the medicare resolution. What we are trying to do is provide services with inadequate resources, and this disturbs me a great deal.
As hon. members will recall, the United Kingdom attempted to introduce this sort of plan before they established medical care in the United Kingdom. It was a plan to increase the strength and number of medical schools. However, the funds were not provided at once and before they knew it medical care was upon them. The medical journals of the United Kingdom and the records of the House of Commons and House of Lords are full of reports that indicate the United Kingdom
(Mr. Brand.]
made a major mistake in not providing facilities before they provided comprehensive medical care.

I believe this is a most important aspect, and I sincerely hope it is not the intention of the government to allow this $500 million and the wonderful idea behind it to be side-tracked and the funds used for something else. I know it is going to cost the Canadian people money but I believe all Canadians will understand that we need these facilities and need this type of care.
I support most earnestly the pleas for increased funds for research which I have heard from every corner of the house. I am sure we will hear more about that. The government increased the funds available for medical research this year, for which I thank them, but the amount is still very small compared with the amount that should be provided for research into the various types of disease.
So far as immigration is concerned, I have pointed out that there will be a considerable drop in the number of immigrant doctors coming to this country over the next few years. I wonder whether the government realizes that by 1986, if our immigration policies about which we have heard so much are successful, we will need somewhere in the neighbourhood of 41,000 doctors in Canada compared with the 24,000 we have now. These figures are based on the ratio of one doctor to every 800 people.
I could go on and discuss other matters that have been covered today but I do not believe any useful purpose would be served. I should like to plead again that the government reconsider the amount of money that is going to be available. They should take a realistic look at the proposals received from the Association of Canadian Medical Colleges, the people who will be most concerned with this problem, to ascertain whether or not the amount of money available can be increased tremendously.
I should like to say a brief word about medical research, to which I referred a moment ago. I point out that in the United
June 14, 1966

States there are 88 medical colleges and 12 in the process of being built. In 1958 the federal government of the United States decided to institute a crash program to strengthen its medical schools by increasing the amount of federal funds available for medical research. As hon. members realize, most medical research is conducted in medical schools. For some years the government of the United States had been providing $250 million for support of medical research. This amount was divided amongst the 88 medical schools. The amount of money available was rapidly expanded until in 1965 that government provided $1.5 billion for research. As a result it has been possible for them to increase rapidly their full-time staff in medical schools. Since they did not have sufficient academically trained individuals in the country it was inevitable that they would look to Canada and the United Kingdom, and that is what they did. As a result we have lost doctors.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Our answer to this must be to provide the facilities for doctors. We must provide them with the medical schools here and we must do so in sufficient quantity so that the brain drain, to use a well known term, does not continue in this country and so that the medical schools and the doctors graduating from them will continue to provide the very highest possible standard of service to the people of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am very pleased to participate in this debate. First I want to say a few words about the brain drain that is concerning many people in the country.
Looking at the figures from various departments and from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics we find that 117,000 immigrant professional workers came to Canada between the years 1946 and 1953. Graduate nurses formed the largest proportion, numbering one in every six persons who came to Canada as immigrant professional workers.
I shall relate my figures to four classes of people with whom we are dealing. They can all be classified as health personnel. I shall quote statistics with regard to dentists, laboratory technicians and assistants, graduate nurses, and physicians and surgeons. In the years 1953 to 1963, 420 dentists, 4,428 laboratory technicians and assistants, 15,359 graduate nurses and 5,032 physicians and surgeons came to Canada as immigrants. It is
Health Resources Fund interesting to note that the doctors and dentists usually came from countries other than the United Kingdom or the United States while laboratory technicians and nurses came mostly from the United Kingdom.
Moving to the question of emigration, which concerns people in Canada even more than immigration, we find that of the professional workers leaving Canada one-quarter are graduate nurses. Using the same four groups of people and the same years, 1953 to 1963, we find that 104 dentists, 3,390 laboratory technicians and assistants, 13,963 graduate nurses and 2,630 physicians and surgeons emigrated from Canada. Therefore, out of the total number of professional emigrants from Canada almost 25 per cent were graduate nurses, 6.1 per cent were laboratory technicians, and almost 5 per cent were physicians and surgeons. We see from the figures the gradually increasing numbers of doctors who are emigrating to the United States. In 1953 doctors represented 4 per cent of professional emigrants and in 1963 this figure had risen to 7 per cent.
Comparing the figures of immigration to Canada and emigration from Canada one sees that there was a net outflow from Canada to the United States in all of the above occupations. Therefore Canada has been losing to the United States but fortunately, as was mentioned by the hon. member for Saskatoon, Canada has been gaining back these groups in that more have emigrated from other countries in the world at large. If one takes the net inflow of these occupations to Canada and subtracts the people in these groups who leave this country to go to the United States, it will be seen that in those years Canada has actually gained 316 dentists, 1,038 laboratory technicians, 1,396 graduate nurses and 2,402 physicians and surgeons.
It is interesting to note that the figures show that one out of every five doctors practising now in Canada is a foreign born, post-war immigrant, as is one dentist out of every 20 and one graduate nurse of every eight. Bringing the value of all this education down to dollars and cents, the figures would indicate a value in the neighbourhood of $450 million.
The brain drain is of great concern to the people of Canada and to the government. I can only reiterate what the hon. member for Saskatoon has already said, that without immigrant doctors coming to Canada our medical profession would have been stretched very far and thin.

June 14, 1966
Health Resources Fund
Interestingly enough, the educational level is higher among the people coming to Canada than among those who are leaving. It should also be noted that Canada gains a great deal from Canadians who are studying abroad as more Canadians study abroad than people from abroad study in Canada. This situation, however, is rapidly reaching a balance.
One of the things we must concern ourselves with is why Canadians with professional training emigrate to the United States. Generally speaking, if one delves into the reasons why people wish to emigrate to the United States one finds that the reasons given are, first, the climate, second, larger incomes in the United States and, third, the fact that some immigrants use Canada as a stepping stone to get into the United States because that country will not allow them to come in directly from their own countries.
For the professional groups the reasons for emigrating are somewhat different. The first reason is the better opportunity in the United States, both in terms of salary and the research facilities which are available; second, because of the free flow of skilled people between Canada and the United States it is often easier for those people to move north or south than it is to move east or west and remain in Canada and, third, again there is the question of climate. Unfortunately we do not have very much control over that. The brain drain is very serious and we all hope that the provisions made by the government in the measure before the house will tend to reverse the trend.
I now want to talk about doctors who are trained in Canada. The medical association is greatly concerned with problems related to this matter and a short time ago published two special editions of their journal which were devoted to medical education. I should like to quote an abstract from "Medical Education, Part I", found in the Canadian Medical Association Journal dated April 2, 1966.
Enrolment in the 12 Canadian medical schools in 1965-66 reached a new high of 4,023, an increase of 3.8 per cent over 1964-65. The percentage of women among medical students (11.4 per cent) was close to that for the preceding two years. The decline in the numbers of students from outside Canada continued into the present year; in 1965-66, 9.1 per cent of medical students were non-Canadian. This decline has been primarily in the number of students from the U.S.A. The number of students from commonwealth countries has shown a steady increase over the seven year period under review; in 1965-66 they make up nearly one-half of all nonCanadian students. It was noted that 27 per cent

of overseas students came to Canada under governmental or intergovernmental sponsorship. Of the Canadian students, 95 per cent came from the "home" provinces of the medical schools.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
It is interesting to compare standards of training in Canada with those of the United States. It is apparent that one of our needs is a better staffing of medical faculties. A comparison between the student-faculty ratio in Canada and the United States reveals a sharp contrast. In the United States there are 6.6 faculty members for every student while in Canada the ratio is 1 to 2.2. Thus the United States has roughly three times as many fulltime faculty members for every student.
It has been said in various publications that a student taking a medical course should have an I.Q. of between 120 and 125. This would encompass approximately 6 per cent of Canadians. I should like to refer to another interesting statement in the Medical Journal. It is from an article entitled "Canadian Applicants For Medical Schools in Canada, 1965-66". The conclusion reached by the author of the article is that it is erroneous to believe there is a surplus of well qualified Canadian applicants at the present time.
I find his conclusion surprising because I had thought there were more well qualified Canadians wishing to take up medicine than were able to do so in the light of our limited facilities. Approximately 10 per cent of all medical students drop out before graduation. There are now 12 medical schools in Canada and two are in the course of construction, in Sherbrooke and Hamilton. It is estimated that we need 440 new doctors each year in order to keep pace with our population growth. We need another 400 to replace doctors who die, retire or fall ill. This means we must find a total of 840 new doctors each year, and we graduate approximately 850 a year. This number is, therefore, only sufficient to keep pace with events, which is not good enough for a country that boasts of an extremely high standard of medical practice, especially bearing in mind recent developments in technology.
Another difficulty which is becoming apparent concerns the role of the general practitioner. In Canada the general practitioner seems to be disappearing. Some people predict he will eventually disappear completely. General practitioners now account for approximately 40 per cent of the total number of doctors, the remainder being specialists of some kind. However, I am glad to say that
June 14, 1966

Health Resources Fund
general practitioners usually spend more than one year at the present time in postgraduate training. In fact, the average is two years.
This brings me to the special concern felt because of the shortage of doctors in rural areas. Not only are more specialists being trained today but general practitioners are increasingly being drawn to practices in well established urban localities rather than in rural areas as was the case years ago. It was common to find efforts to attract doctors to rural communities. A community would provide rent-free facilities and other benefits of a fringe nature to encourage doctors to come to the area.
In 1960 the ratio of doctors to patients in Canada was approximately one to 904. Some people think this ratio should be one in every 750. The ratio of dentists to patients is roughly one to 3,000 and most dental authorities think it should probably be one to 2,000. There is one nurse for every 260 of the population and most authorities think the proportion should be one to every 200. So there is a need to train more and more people in these fields and we certainly welcome the grants which the federal government intends to make available to help provide training facilities.
It has been estimated, I hope accurately, that with the help of the increased facilities provided by the medical schools the medical student population should double by 1970. This should be the aim, and if it means the spending of even more money by the federal government then I would certainly support it.
One important aspect of this whole subject concerns wages and salaries. In the last Civil Service Commission circular, a copy of which goes to members of parliament, I noticed an advertisement for an elevator maintenance and inspection officer for which post the salary offered was $9,000 a year. But for chemists, bacteriologists and pharmacists the salary offered was approximately $7,000 a year. I am not against paying a reasonable wage to an elevator inspector or maintenance officer but I suggest that a qualified chemist, bacteriologist or pharmacist should certainly command a higher salary than persons in that category. I am sure the hon. member for Simcoe East could give even more surprising examples. When I graduated from the University of Toronto in 1951 the salary paid to junior internes by the Toronto General Hospital-it was not even called a salary; it was called an honorarium-amounted to $100 a year, the price per day of a pack of
cigarettes for a person in a highly responsible position and on call 24 hours a day.
I am glad to say that the situation has altered. Nevertheless, salaries have still not reached a level appropriate to the work these doctors are doing, the hours they must put in and the responsibility they carry. The same is true of nurses and other trained personnel.
Before closing I should like to make six recommendations. I am aware that most of them do not fall within the jurisdiction of the federal government but I put them forward, in the hope that those concerned will take cognizance of them and follow them up in order that sufficient health personnel may be available in Canada when we put a full medical care scheme into effect.
My first suggestion, to which I have already referred, is that higher salaries be paid to doctors and nurses in their training period. Though Canadian hospitals may pay $100 a month, one can pick up journals carrying advertisements for positions in the United States where internes are paid $5,000 and more. I am satisfied that when the government has an opportunity to look at the matter again and pays attention to the representations made to it year after year by the most qualified people in this field it will realize that it will have to double or quadruple this amount.
I want to deal just with the subject of medical research. Through its national institute on health the government of the United States is spending over $1 billion a year on medical research. Canada has approximately one-tenth of the population of the United States and to come anywhere close to the United States we should be spending $100 million a year on medical research alone. Mr. Chairman, the debate this
afternoon on the need for a health resources fund has been of a constructive nature and I hope that my remarks will follow the general precedent set by those speakers who have preceded me. As mentioned by the minister in his introductory remarks this afternoon, this resolution is a preliminary step to the introduction of a national medicare program. I believe all members will recognize the necessity of moving immediately into the planning stage of this program. I believe that the minister said we should initiate the planning at once by way of the establishment of a health resources fund so we will have to the greatest extent possible-I appreciate that we may not achieve perfection at all times in

June 14, 1966
Health Resources Fund this matter-the trained personnel and facilities for training personnel who will be available to service the health plan when it is introduced, I hope next year, on a national basis.
In my remarks, Mr. Chairman, I want to take a general and pragmatic approach to the subject of the health resources fund and discuss, as I have already mentioned, the necessity of moving ahead with this legislation as quickly as we can in order that we will be in a position to implement and carry out the provisions of the medicare program which will be implemented next year. This will be important social legislation and it is important for us in the parliament of Canada to do what we can to ensure that this social legislation will go into operation effectively and smoothly when it is introduced.
I do not subscribe to the argument which I believe was advanced by the hon. member for Saskatoon that we should not proceed with a national medicare program until we have reached the state of perfection where we have all the trained personnel necessary to put it into effect. It is my belief that we are never going to reach a state of utopia where we will have all the personnel and facilities we would like to have but that we should do the best we can in this matter and move ahead as quickly as is reasonably possible.
The resolution we are debating this afternoon proposes the setting up of a $500 million fund to be expended over a period of 15 years. As the minister said in introducing the resolution, the basic purpose is to help meet the greater need for trained people to provide medical care services and to endeavour to catch up where possible in areas where adequate trained personnel are in short supply. This fund will also supply moneys to support the construction and equipment of facilities for health research and training. It will provide capital grants for the construction, renovation and basic equipment of research establishments, teaching schools, medical schools and training facilities for essential health services personnel.
On three or four occasions this afternoon there has been an expression of opinion and regret in this debate from those opposite-I appreciate that it is informed opinion particularly because much of it has come from members of the medical profession-that the legislation which we are now considering will be too little, too late. I think that was the expression of one of the speakers. I am not personally wedded to the proposition that this

program will be an end in itself. I think we will have to proceed on the basis of experience. We will have to proceed and see what we can achieve with the money available to us which we are prepared to expend in pursuance of the objectives of this resolution, if it should transpire that we are not graduating the number of trained personnel required to implement our health services program, if we do not have the facilities to ensure that Canadians have the right to take advantage of the program, then parliament will have to look at this proposition again. But for the time being I think we are taking a reasonable and responsible approach to this matter.
In his introductory remarks the minister referred, as did my hon. friend from Halton, to the part the provinces will be expected to play in this program. I want to take a minute or two to deal with this question and particularly with the constitutional aspect of the responsibility of the provinces in the supplying of funds to further the objectives we are trying to achieve in this resolution. I know the minister has been in consultation with the health ministers of the provinces and that this matter has been under discussion. I am a little concerned in this respect. I would feel more at ease if the resolution itself were worded in a little firmer or more definitive fashion. I have reference to the portion of the resolution which says "it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the establishment of a health resources fund to assist provinces in the acquisition", and so on. I emphasize the words "to assist provinces". Further, Mr. Chairman, I am concerned about the reference in the resolution to "such amounts as from time to time are required and to provide for contributions therefrom to the provinces".
I appreciate, as my hon. friend from Halton has already pointed out, that constitutionally there are some responsibilities resting on the provinces in this area. I raise this matter now only to say to the minister that it is my hope he will keep in mind in his further negotiations with the provinces that they have a responsibility which they should assume in this matter as we are, I think, assuming our responsibility by the introduction of this legislation. I mention this matter, as I say, because as representatives of the federal authority we are today considering, and I hope will today pass, a resolution which will provide for a substantial contribution to the implementation of health services in this

Mr. Chairman, like many
other members who have risen this afternoon I, too, rise to support this resolution in principle. It is extremely interesting to me, sir, to realize that we are debating this issue at a time when the question of medicare is foremost in our minds. I also support the principle of medicare just as I support the principle of this resolution. I speak, I think, for many members in all corners of the house when I say that I am sick and tired of seeing people have their life savings wiped out after a few months of illness. I believe that the program of medicare which the minister is putting before the house, coupled with provincial action, will go a long way toward alleviating the situation in which so many Canadians find themselves today, namely, seeing their life savings dissipated overnight as a result of sickness.
I thought I should like to bring this point to the attention of the house. Intention and reality are two different things. When the British brought in their national health plan years ago they really had to wrestle with what we recognize now as a shortage of medical manpower. In bringing this problem to the minister's attention today and in looking back at the British experience, I think we will realize we have a great lesson to learn. Whether or not the officials of the Canadian
June 14, 1966

Medical Association who conferred with the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Health and Welfare last week indicated they were effectively supporting the principle of medicare, I think they indicated to the minister that even independently of medicare our nation is facing an imminent crisis related to a shortage of medical manpower.
What I am going to say could be debated but I will make this declaration: What we are dealing with today is a long-term measure but even as a long-term measure I do not think it goes far enough to deal with the situation. But if we are not going to be faced with a real dilemma we need an emergency crash program today, immediately, in order to avert the imminent crisis relating to the shortage of doctors in this country. Last year, as the hon. member for Simcoe East has continually pointed out, 800 doctors went to the United States. Their earning power annually represented $400 million and it cost this country on the average $25,000 to educate these doctors. I reiterate that Canada is losing these doctors, this medical manpower, and unless immediate action is taken we shall be faced with a real crisis within two years. The long-term measure we are discussing today does not take that into consideration.
As many of us know, when the family doctor in the smaller centres passes on he is not replaced. Last year hundreds of qualified applicants were turned down at our medical schools. In 1965 these schools turned out approximately the same number of doctors as they did ten years ago. About 4 per cent of all the doctors who graduated in 1965 left the country. Some time ago many doctors were coming to our country because of dissatisfaction with working conditions in their native lands. This situation no longer exists. Not only do we lack medical schools but some of the existing schools have recently been found to be below proper accreditation standards. Before we embark on a medicare program we need to give consideration to the fact that Canada ranks only twentieth in the world in relation to the doctor to population ratio.
Today we have 1,000 teachers in our medical schools. If we want to maintain present standards, excluding all the doctors involved in medicare we must by 1970 have at least 2,000 teachers in our schools. Yet our teachers continue to move to the United States. Why is this so. The major reason lies in the fact that there are improved research facilities there. As has been stated this afternoon, improved
Health Resources Fund research is being done in the United States medical schools. The United States federal government is responsible for 90 per cent of the financial support for research in these schools. Federal assistance in the United States last year in this regard amounted to $1,300 million, while in the same year the federal share in Canada amounted to approximately $15 million. Who can wonder at the fact that our medical teachers continue to go to the United States? This exodus must be stopped, Mr. Chairman. The long-term measure we are discussing today will not stop it.
I shall try to finish before six o'clock, Mr. Chairman. Our medical schools should reevaluate their position. They have a job to do in connection with this situation. The federal government could greatly increase its assistance to medical research in Canada. This should be done right away, independently of the measure we are discussing, if this crash emergency program is going to avert a crisis. The province of Ontario, for example, has a five year plan under which they will spend $500 million to enlarge existing medical schools and construct new ones. These schools will be mere shells unless we have teachers to staff them. We must remember that research attracts teachers. The difference between having sufficient excellent teachers and having none is medical research.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to delay the passage of this resolution unduly but there are one or two observations I should like to make on this important measure.
Most hon. members have been critical of the fact that only $500 million has been allocated to this project. I agree that the

June 14. 1966
Health Resources Fund amount should be larger, but in all fairness I feel that the minister and the government should be congratulated on the start which has been made. We agree that $500 million will not be sufficient but it is a start and I have a notion that once this project is under way additional money will be made available as required.
I am concerned about the division which will be made of this sum when the time comes to divide it. Several times I have had occasion to sit around a conference table when federal funds were being divided and my experience has been that unfortunately in many cases it is a case of "dog eat dog".
I am especially reminded of what happened in 1957 when the federal government of that day made a substantial grant available to the Atlantic provinces. It was decided that the division of the grant should be arranged by the provinces themselves, and the premiers or their financial advisers met to divide this adjustment grant. The result was very unfair so far as the province of Prince Edward Island was concerned. The money was divided on the basis of 30 per cent to Nova Scotia, 30 per cent to New Brunswick, 30 per cent to Newfoundland and only 10 per cent to Prince Edward Island. I hope that when the time comes to allocate this $500 million among the provinces it will not be done on a per capita basis but rather on the basis of fiscal need which is the only fair system of allocation.
I have a suggestion which I shall make to the minister for what its worth. It is that when the time comes to divide this money a certain amount be set aside to be divided on a per capita basis. I agree that this should be done. Having done this, a further sum should be set aside to be divided on the basis of fiscal need. I think we have a friend in court because the Minister of National Health and Welfare comes from the Atlantic provinces. I believe, too, that an additional amount should be set aside as a special grant to the Atlantic provinces.
It is in the Atlantic provinces that the fiscal need really arises. We do not have the tax potential which exists in other parts of Canada and unless some recognition is given to our special fiscal need we shall not be able to share in the benefits of this legislation as fairly as we ought.
I was interested in the statement of the minister that the objective of the fund is to catch up in places where supplies of adequately trained personnel are not presently available. This is most important and I hope

something can be done by means of this program to encourage doctors to settle in sparsely populated areas such as country districts. I have in mind particularly my own district where we are served by only one medical doctor. It is frightening at times to think that a district of such a size is served by only one medical doctor. Efforts have been made by the people themselves to encourage doctors to come there but for some reason or other doctors do not want to settle in these sparsely populated places.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
I do not know what the incentive can be. Possibly it could be in the form of a tax incentive. We offer tax incentives to industries to settle in areas in which ordinarily they might not be inclined to settle. Something in the form of a tax incentive over a five year period might be made available to doctors to encourage them to settle in areas in which otherwise they might not be inclined to practise.
Such a program would have to be clearly defined. There would have to be a definition of an area suffering from the lack of medical service and some arrangement would have to be made whereby doctors would enter into contracts to stay there for a stated period of time, say five, six or ten years. The time is coming when the government will have to consider providing an incentive of some kind to encourage young men leaving medical schools to settle in areas not properly serviced by doctors.
We in our small province do not hope to benefit from this fund by the setting up of medical schools. The size of our province does not warrant a medical school. We are adequately served by Dalhousie and by the medical school at McGill for those who choose to go there, but something could be done in our province in the field of medical research.
One of the reasons doctors are not inclined to settle in areas less thickly populated than cities is that they have no research facilities at their disposal, and a young man coming out of medical school wants to continue to improve his status and education. Unless there are facilities available to do so he will not settle in isolated areas.
I hope an adequate share of this $500 million will be given to our province for assistance in research. In recent years we have made encouraging advances in Prince Edward Island in research into mental health and mental retardation. Such research could

I realize the reasons are many. One very obvious one is the fact that more and more men who graduate as general practitioners go on to become specialists and therefore their services are too specialized for them to serve in a rural area. Of course others are anxious to serve in areas where there may be research facilities and where they will have opportunities to consult.
I think one of the fundamental problems is that which concerns education itself. Unfortunately because of our own experience and training we are very much of the opinion that when a man graduates from medical school by and large he has completed his education and goes forth to serve wherever he is called upon to do so. The problem, particularly today, is that medical knowledge is expanding at such a rate that what a man may be equipped to do this year may be completely out of date four or five years from now; so much will have been added that he may feel almost unable to exercise his practice successfully. When a man goes to a rural area it becomes a real problem for him to keep in touch with the latest developments. He is not meeting and talking every day to

people who are in touch with all the recent
changes. He is not caught up in the kind of intellectual milieu which will assist him to keep up with medical practice. Therefore he feels he really is putting himself behind the eight-ball, not just financially but in terms of his own effective service, by going out into a rural practice.
