We took a great deal of interest in the field of medical research and it was during our term of office as the government that the Medical Research Council was set up separate and apart from the National Research Council under which it had functioned for a great many years. I was prepared to bring forward a bill to establish the Medical Research Council in its own right just as the National Research Council is established by statute. Unfortunately the people of Canada had ideas which differed from ours and they changed the government of the country. That step has not yet been taken.
Nevertheless the Medical Research Council for the last several years has been administering its own budget and special funds which have been allocated to that council. These amounts are now shown separately in the estimates each year whereas in the years prior to 1961 they were not easily discovered because they were combined with those of the National Research Council.
May I point out to the hon. member for Winnipeg North that in the 44th annual report of the National Research Council of Canada, 1960-61, page 33, will be found the report of the Medical Research Council given by the late Dr. Farquharson. Just to indicate the development may I read one or two paragraphs from his report:
In the last two decades also, government support of medical research has been increased greatly in an attempt to meet expanding needs. In 1938 the first associate committee on medical research of the National Research Council had a budget of $53,000.
We have come a very long way since 1938. I continue to quote:
After the war a division of medical research was established, with an initial budget of approximately $200,000. With the rapid growth of medical research in our universities, the budget was gradually increased to some $900,000 by 1957.
That was the year that the Progressive Conservative party took over the government of this country. Then the learned doctor stated:
A sharper increase in the last three years brought it to $2,300,000. Virtually all these funds have been used in the training of scientists and the support of medical research in the universities and their associated institutes and hospitals; the National Research Council maintained no medical laboratories of its own.

adequate now, but we support the resolution presently before us because we recognize the need, within the limitation of funds available, to provide for medical research.
The funds made available were more than doubled in three years and the amount has been increasing steadily ever since. The present government continues to recognize the need. By 1959-60, the total government funds for support of extramural research had risen to approximately $5,000,000-

ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED

speechtext:
Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of National
Health and Welfare) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure, to be known as the Canada Assistance Plan, to establish a program for sharing with the provinces in the cost of assistance, including health care and welfare services, provided to or in respect of persons in need, including mothers and children, older persons, disabled persons and unemployed persons who are in need, and in the cost of developing and improving assistance and welfare services programs
Canada Assistance Plan
including child and youth welfare programs throughout Canada; to provide for the making of arrangements for extending provincial welfare programs, with the approval of Indian bands, to Indians with reserve status, and for the making of payments to the provinces with respect to the cost of so extending those programs; to provide for the making of payments to the provinces with respect to the cost of specialized projects for assisting and rehabilitating persons in need or likely to become persons in need who have unusual difficulty in obtaining or holding employment; to provide for amendments to the Old Age Assistance Act, the Blind Persons Act, the Disabled Persons Act, and the Unemployment Assistance Act that are incidental to or consequential on the introduction of the Canada Assistance Plan; and to provide further for the extension of the Established Programs (Interim Arrangements) Act to the Canada Assistance Plan.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Batten in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to be able to speak to the resolution dealing with the Canada Assistance Plan. In doing so, I can say that the resolution deals with an area that has been the subject of extensive federal-provincial discussions over the past few years. It is also an area in which there is a remarkable degree of agreement on the need for action and the essentials of the approach that should be taken.
The basic features of the Canada Assistance Plan, as set out in the resolution, were outlined in the house by the Prime Minister on April 6, 1965 when he described the various measures being proposed to increase opportunity and reduce poverty.
The Prime Minister referred at the time to the discussions that had been held with the provinces up to that point in developing proposals. Since then the plan has been considered at two federal-provincial conferences of ministers of welfare.
Briefly stated, the Canada Assistance Plan will provide: a basis for co-ordinating public assistance programs in Canada; federal sharing for the first time in mothers' allowance programs; federal support for the strengthening of administration and welfare services related to social assistance programs; emphasis on developing, improving and extending services designed to lessen the amount of dependency; federal aid for buttressing child and youth welfare services; federal sharing of health care costs for social assistance recipients; no federal ceilings on benefits under this new program and full sharing of payments made on the basis of need to improve the level of benefits now being paid to the aged, the blind and the disabled.

June 14, 1966
Canada Assistance Plan
The Canada Assistance Plan will mean an additional cost to the federal treasury in this fiscal year of $85 million, bringing federal outlays on public assistance and welfare services to more than one quarter of a billion dollars. This is a program which carried the endorsement of all provincial governments at the federal-provincial conference earlier this year.
I do not propose to review the background of this measure in detail. It is worth noting, however, that the federal government and the provinces have been working co-operatively for 40 years in the provision of public assistance to persons in need. These joint efforts began with the old age pensions program of 1927 and were followed by pensions for the blind in 1937, the old age assistance program of 1951, and the disabled persons allowances program of 1954. These we have come to refer to as the categorical allowance programs. With the adoption of the unemployment assistance program in 1956 and its amendments in 1957, the federal government undertook to share in responsibility for the provision of general assistance to a broader group of employable and unemployable persons.
As a result of this sequence of events, the federal government is now sharing with the provinces in assistance to persons in need under four separate programs, three of which-those for the aged, the blind and the disabled-base eligibility on a means test. The fourth, unemployment assistance, employs the needs test.
The logic of moving toward an integrated approach to public assistance has been widely recognized. This step has been recommended by many welfare organizations, including the Canadian Welfare Council. It has also been advocated by the Auditor General and, in 1964, by the public accounts committee which recommended "that consideration should be given to including with unemployment assistance other existing programs to assist the needy so as to provide better co-ordination of federal-provincial efforts in this field."
The movement away from special or categorical assistance toward general assistance programs began in some provinces in the early 1950's and has continued at differing rates since then. In some, it has taken the form of integrating all provincially administered measures for persons requiring assistance on a long term basis because of age, disability or family responsibility in the absence of the principal breadwinner.
XMr. MacEachen.]
While encouraging the movement toward comprehensive programs based on need, it is the government's intention to continue to provide for contributions under the existing categorical programs for the aged, the blind and the disabled. This will enable provinces to retain these measures if they wish, or to phase them out on a gradual basis. I should also point out that under existing agreements the federal government must give ten years notice if it wishes to discontinue its contributions under any of these categorical programs.
In addition to providing for the integration of existing programs, the plan will provide for the payment of assistance on the basis of need. The needs test considers the actual requirements of individuals and families, as well as their resources, in determining the amount of assistance to be provided. This is in contrast to the means test which relates assistance to income and assets.
A major limitation of the unemployment assistance program was that it excluded one of the largest categories of persons in need, namely mothers with dependent children. The Canada Assistance Plan corrects this anomaly by providing for federal contributions toward the costs of assistance to some 200,000 mothers and children who have not previously been covered under a federal measure. Through this extension, the federal government will be providing an estimated $27 million of new funds to the provinces and will further support the integration of mothers' allowances programs into comprehensive assistance measures. In the past year, some provinces have already increased rates of benefits for needy mothers, and I believe that the anticipated introduction of the Canada Assistance Plan was helpful in encouraging this action. We are hopeful that the addition of federal aid will do much to assist needy mothers and children both now and in the years to come.
I would like to refer briefly to the other areas to be covered under the Canada Assistance Plan. Coverage of health care services for persons in need is an essential feature of the plan and constitutes federal recognition of the importance of such services in any program that seeks to alleviate or prevent poverty. It is intended that the plan will cover any range of medical and associated health services, including drugs and dental and optical care, that the provinces choose to offer. The cost of this extension will, of course depend on the nature and extent of
June 14, 1966

the programs adopted by the provinces. Our present estimate of federal contributions to the provinces for such services is some $22 million for the current fiscal year. The medical care costs under this program will, of course, be reduced with the coming into effect of the medicare plan.
The plan will provide for federal contributions toward the costs of improving and extending welfare services, including services provided either through public welfare departments or, under certain conditions, by voluntary agencies. Welfare services are intended to include those services that have as their object the lessening, removal or prevention of the causes and effects of poverty, child neglect or dependence on public assistance. Examples of such services include casework, counselling, assessment and referral services, adoption services, homemakers and day care services, and community development. The federal contribution to the provinces under this part of the plan is expected to be several million dollars for the current fiscal year.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
An important consideration in developing a measure with strong preventive emphasis is that it should make appropriate provision for the needs of children and youth. With this in mind, the plan has been extended to cover maintenance costs for children in the care of child welfare authorities. Health care and welfare services will similarly be extended to such children. The estimated cost of this item for 1966-67 is some $16 million.
The plan-that is the Canada Assistance Plan-will provide for separate agreements with provinces for the extension of provincial welfare programs to Indians who are now living on reserves, crown lands, or in unorganized territory. Provincial programs will be extended only with the consent of the Indian bands involved and the agreements will be along the lines of the draft agreement tabled in the house by my colleague, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, on January 19, 1966.
This measure is intended to provide Indians, for whom services are now largely provided by the federal government, with the same access to provincial assistance and welfare service programs as is available to other provincial residents. As such, it represents a significant step toward enabling Indians to take full advantage of the community services available to the general population.
Canada Assistance Plan Since the incidence of need for Indians is greater than for the balance of the population, the agreements will contain a special sharing formula to enable provinces to assume responsibility for Indian assistance and welfare services without incurring burdensome costs.
An agreement of the type contemplated by the plan has recently been entered into with the province of Ontario, and I hope that with the assurance of an appropriate federal contribution toward their costs, other provinces will undertake to extend their welfare programs to Indians.
Another feature of the plan which emphasizes its rehabilitative approach is its provision for work activity projects. These are projects designed to provide socially useful activity to help persons in need move toward self-support. The projects would be for persons who are apparently fit to work, but who, because of environmental, personal or family reasons, are unable to obtain or retain employment or to take advantage of the various vocational rehabilitation and training measures designed to help improve their work capacities. These work activity programs will also be for persons, such as the severely retarded, who have limited employment potential which can be developed if they are given opportunity for some form of meaningful activity.
This part of the plan is experimental in its approach and will require close co-ordination with other measures having to do with employment and vocational rehabilitation. Thus reimbursement will be on a project basis.
In the course of my remarks, Mr. Chairman, I have referred to five areas-assistance for needy mothers, health care, welfare services and child welfare and work activity-in which new federal funds will be made available to the provinces. While these additional funds are largely directed to programs now being provincially financed, and may be thought of as savings to the provinces, it is the hope of the government that the provinces will use these funds to make improvements in their assistance and welfare service programs. I am happy to see evidence that this is already being done in several provinces.
We estimate that these new federal contributions, when taken with the additional outlays that are anticipated as a direct result of improvements made by the provinces, will amount to some $85 million in 1966-67. The full impact on federal expenditures will be
June 14. 1966

Canada Assistance Plan felt as provinces are able to strengthen and improve their programs in accordance with the purposes of this plan.
Another feature of the plan is that it will make funds available to the provinces to supplement those cases where existing social welfare benefits fall short of budgetary needs. It should be noted that improvements can be made not only through more adequate cash benefits, but also through more ready access to health care and welfare services. The value of such services cannot be overrated in enabling the recipients of these programs to maintain the fullest possible degree of independence in the community.
The resolution refers to amendments to the Old Age Assistance Act, the Blind Persons Act and the Disabled Persons Act. Under the amendments, the provinces will be able to discontinue these programs, either wholly or in part, and to assist persons who would otherwise qualify for allowances under these acts through general assistance measures coming under the Canada Assistance Plan. I should make it clear that where persons now receiving such allowances are transferred, provision will be made for them to receive assistance in amounts at least comparable to their present benefits.
The resolution also refers to the extension of the terms of the Established Programs (Interim Arrangements) Act to the Canada Assistance Plan. This means that a province that has taken advantage of the contracting-out provisions of that act may take the same step in relation to the Canada Assistance Plan. This provision is consistent with existing arrangements under the Established Programs (Interim Arrangements) Act which cover old age assistance, blind persons allowances, disabled persons allowances and unemployment assistance.
To sum up, legislation is being proposed to provide for a comprehensive program of assistance and welfare services for persons requiring public support for one reason or another. This plan complements social insurance measures such as unemployment insurance and the Canada Pension Plan and it provides an underpinning for our whole social security structure. It is a matter of great satisfaction to me that the plan, as announced, has received general and enthusiastic support from public authorities and voluntary agencies across Canada.
[Mr. MacEachen.l

Mr. Chairman, may I say first of all that I think the plan before us is a good plan. I feel, none the less, that its framework was started some years ago by the hon. member for Perth when he was minister of national health and welfare. It is true that we had means, one way or another, of helping, with the exception of the 200,000 mothers, all those persons fitting into the categories that the minister mentioned. Including the mothers in this manner is well worth while.
I am disappointed that the minister has not seen fit to raise the old age pension to $100 a month. Pensioners are the forgotten people. If all the promises made during the last election about a Canadian assistance act and the war on poverty came true, there would be no poverty-and there would be no money to look after it. There are many aspects of this question-old age pensions, disabled persons pensions, various kinds of welfare programs, the training and retraining of young people and welfare programs affecting mothers and children. Then, of course, the decline in the value of the dollar has brought about the erosion of the value of savings of all pensioners and other people.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
I will deal first with old age security. The Senate committee in its report said no means test should be applied to old age pensioners. They brought this out dramatically. It has definitely been proven that 70 per cent of women and 60 per cent of the men have no other income than old age pension at the age of 70. This leaves only 30 per cent of the women and 40 per cent of the men as possible subjects for a means test.
If hon. members look up the figures relating to the incomes of these pensioners as they are to be found in figures produced by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics I think they will be persuaded that it is not worth while submitting these people to the humiliation of an inquiry into their affairs. Or is there some
June 14, 1966

economic reason for it? This is one of the statements made in the Senate report on aging. One of the submissions in that report was-and the committee was most emphatic on this point-that the old age pensioner must not be subjected to the humiliation of a means or needs test. I believe most of us in this chamber, including the minister, will say the Senate was right.
How can we propose to apply a means test to these people whose savings have been taken away from year to year by the erosion of money values? I would like to think that this government wishes to make amends. I am not excusing the Conservatives, but a Liberal government has been in power for 25 of the 31 years in which the savings of those who are now pensioners were being eroded-and Liberal erosion was always higher.
Let us bear in mind that those who are pensioners today had completed half of their working lives by 1940 when wages were about 40 cents an hour, if you had a job, and that the dollar they earned then has now a purchasing power of only 37 cents.
I wonder why we are so dilatory and derelict about doing something for these people whose money we have eroded year after year-a hidden form of taxation which is a terrible form of taxation for persons living on fixed incomes. It is impossible to gauge the amount. One year it is 2 per cent. Another year it is 4 per cent, or 5 per cent. It takes its toll every year of their savings, of the value of their government bonds, of their life insurance policies and so on. It is our duty to see that justice is done to these people.
I wonder why the government did not pay more attention to the Senate report on aging. I think it was a very fine report. These pensioners are proud people. Many of them have been through two world wars. They do not want to come begging for their rights to this House of Commons. Many are too proud to come and ask. They would not want to suffer the humiliation. They would just go on tightening their belts, eating a little less and spending a little less on clothes and the other things they need so badly.
I do not see how this government can have
the audacity to face the old people of this country with a means test or a needs test -because there is no difference. Why have hon. members opposite discarded their Liberal principles? You were in the house, Mr. Chairman, when Mr. St. Laurent brought
Canada Assistance Plan down the old age security bill which was made to apply universally. There was no means test or needs test. Why? Simply because he understood the feelings of those who would benefit and their wish to avoid humiliation. In the second place the parliament of that they day knew that income tax would apply to those who were getting more than they should. He made the benefits available to everyone. Why have hon. gentlemen opposite departed so far from Liberal principles? I wonder whether the government realizes that the pensioner of today went through one of the great depressions of this world from 1928 to 1940. These are the people who are now being denied $100 a month.
There is another principle involved. These people are growing older. There is more sickness among them, more degenerative processes requiring treatment by drugs-and today's drug prices bear no relation to what their earnings were.
There are rays of hope occasionally, and we do see a ray of hope. There is some indication that the government is beginning to listen to the opposition. An article in the Globe and Mail last Monday says this:
The government had resisted efforts by the opposition parties in the Commons to raise old-age pensions to $100 a month. But an increasing number of Liberal members, led by cabinet ministers, are arguing that something must be done to aid old folk.
Next it argued that there should be no increase in the pension while attempts are being made to place a lid on wage increases which would add to inflation.
But now the construction workers in Montreal, the Quebec longshoremen and the seaway workers are heading toward pay raises exceeding 30 per cent.
Many Liberals feel it is unjust that economic groups with political muscle should be able to improve their economic position by striking, or threatening to strike, while old persons are denied an increase in the admittedly inadequate pension.
Legislation to implement the Canada Assistance Plan will be introduced shortly.
Well, we have arrived.
This will provide that pensioners proving need will be able to draw benefits raising their total allowance to more than $100 a month. But old persons have told the government bluntly that they are not interested in this plan; they want their pensions as a right and without having to show need.
Surely they should not be required to do so, when, looking back over the record, we can see that the working years of so many of them were spent before 1940, when wages

Mr. Chairman, as the Minister of National Health and Welfare reminded us, it was in April, 1965, 14 months ago, that the Prime Minister sounded the trumpet and told us about the Canada Assistance Plan. At long last we have the legislation for this plan before parliament.
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
The Minister of National Health and Welfare has a very winsome voice. He has also a capacity for picking words; and when you add that capacity to that voice it makes us feel we have something. But when one looks at the package which has been outlined tonight he wonders whether it was really worth the sound of the trumpet. I have been looking through some of the speeches made about the Canada Assistance Plan by the former minister of national health and welfare, by the present Minister of National Health and Welfare, and by no less a person than his parliamentary secretary. I should like to draw attention to one sentence in a speech made by the parliamentary secretary in Fredericton on June 2 of this year. Speaking of the Canada Assistance Plan she said:
...I would like to make two general points; the first is that the plan does not involve any grand new programs.
How right she was.
It is, rather, an attempt to re-organize and redirect existing programs and fashion a comprehensive social assistance system that will reflect the needs and problems of today.
Later she said:
The second point is that although the plan will operate under the umbrella of a federal statute, and will receive substantial financial support from the federal government, the specific details of the various programs and the responsibility for administering them will rest with the provinces.
Even after one says the nice things that can be said about this legislation-and I am going to say them-the fact is that we have just shuffled the deck a bit; we have just done a little re-organizing of our services. We have not come through with any "grand new programs"-and I quote my hon. friend from Westmorland. As a matter of fact even the amount of money that is involved-and the hon. member for Grey-Bruce pinned the minister down on that-indicates that there really is not as much to this program as we have been led to believe there was.
DEBATES	6413
Canada Assistance Plan
Now, Mr. Chairman, I said there were some good things in the Canada Assistance Plan and I wish to take a minute or two to emphasize the things about this legislation which I think are good. I think it is most encouraging to learn there has been a wide measure of federal-provincial agreement on what is being done. I think the more federal-provincial co-operation we can have in the welfare field, the better for Canada as a whole. I think also it is very much to be commended that the federal government is prepared to share financially in a number of programs in which up to this point there has been no federal financial participation. I do not know yet-and we will not know until we have the details-how this $85 million breaks down, or how much federal money is going into these various fields. But even if it is only the beginning, I welcome the fact that there will be federal participation in such things as mothers' allowances, the administration of social welfare services, work in the field of dependency, homemaker services, day care, Indian welfare programs, rehabilitation, and so on.
I think the more we weld together these programs and have federal-provincial cooperation and federal financial participation in these programs, the better for all concerned. I listened carefully, when the minister was referring to things to be done for children, to hear whether or not he would have anything to say about some of the information which recently has reached us about the problems of mentally disturbed children. Right in this province of Ontario we have learned some things which have been disturbing to us. I would hope that at a later stage the minister might be able to tell us whether any of this federal money that is to be used in our participation in these various programs will be available for assistance in this general area.
So I say, Mr. Chairman, it is good that we are going to get our social welfare programs on some sort of a basis of wider co-operation. I welcome that; but I am afraid, as one who had looked forward to the Canada Assistance Plan very hopefully, that I do not feel as encouraged or as optimistic about it as I might have been. I hope the minister will accept that as a challenge.
He says that sometimes I probe his social conscience and give him sleepless nights.

The minister says he has had several sleepless nights in the last few days. I hope he will have one tonight and come back with a great deal more substance to this measure when we get to the bill. Also I should like to say that to the extent we are moving from means' tests to needs tests, with regard to programs which now have means tests, this is all to the good. Sometimes people wonder whether a change of name makes for any real difference, but in the field of social work it does make a difference. A needs test is more humane and more realistic than a means test. I am glad to know that in programs such as old age assistance, blind persons allowances and disabled persons allowances we are going to move from a means test to a more advanced approach, namely the needs test.
Having said that I want to say something pretty specific and forthright about the position of our older people. The first thing I wish to say, I have to say without having heard much from the minister tonight as to what the plan is going to do for older people. I do not want to see any kind of test brought back with regard to our older people. It took us a long time to get rid of the means test. With all respect to my good friend from Sirncoe East, Mr. St. Laurent did not give that legislation quite as generously and easily as my hon. friend suggested tonight. He was not here but I was. I remember Mr. St. Laurent standing up and saying he could not conceive of the idea that he at the age of 70 would get a pension without a means test; but in 1950 we did bring in the kind of report to which the government had to pay some attention. We got rid of the means test from the pension payable to people at age 70 and over.
Now we have the Canada Pension Plan which provides pensions from age 65 on for people who have been employed. They can take the pension between the ages of 65 and 70 or at age 70. In connection with pensions under the Canada Pension Plan there is no means test. I think it is progress that today we have got to the place where people, when they retire, receive their pensions as of right without any means test. I do not think we should take the backward step of imposing any kind of a test, call it a needs test or what you will, so far as old people are concerned. If we start saying the way to provide extra money for our older people is under some kind of a needs test, then the pressure will be on to leave the $75 old age security level

where it is for all time, whereas I think what we should be doing is pushing up that $75 level to at least $100 a month now, and indeed still further later on.
What troubles me tonight, Mr. Chairman -and perhaps this is the reason I cannot get up and give the minister a soporific and complimentary speech-is the way in which he skated around this question of what is going to be done for our older people. Is it that there is something in the legislation which he is ashamed of? Once or twice he made reference to this legislation as having in it something for the aged. He referred to the Old Age Assistance Act, but did not once refer to the Old Age Security Act and did not once give us any details.

I find this passing strange in view of a number of speeches that have been made by Liberals on the subject of what the Canada Assistance Plan was going to do for our older people. All of us who went through the last election campaign remember what the Prime Minister replied to those of us in other parties who were calling for an increase in old age security pensions to $100 a month. He said that if you voted Liberal you might get $125 a month; there might be a needs test, and it might be given under the Canada Assistance Plan; but you would get more money if you managed to meet the test under the Liberal program than under the programs of any of the other parties.
Not only was that the kind of thing the Liberals said during the election campaign, but they made similar statements in several speeches. I have not got them all with me but I do have four of them. The rest are in my flies upstairs, but I have been saving them.
The former minister of national health and welfare, the present Secretary of State, set the pattern by a typical speech she made on May 20, 1965, at Charlottetown. She said this, among other things:
One of the things that is often forgotten when the Canada Assistance Plan is being discussed is that it can provide additional assistance for people who are already receiving old age security.

I was listening very closely. There were references to the aged and to the Old Age Assistance Act, but there was no reference that I heard to extra money being made available to people who are in receipt of old age security. Let me quote from a speech the present minister made to the Ottawa Welfare Council on May 4, 1966. He said in part:
The basic aim of the Canada Assistance Plan is to remove the anomalies from present programs. As a result, the federal government will share in payments higher than the present $75 a month limit in cases where more help is needed. And, needless to say, the assistance will be available in addition to the present $75 a month old age security pension.
I have another speech which seems to be the same as the one made by the former minister and by the parliamentary secretary. This speech was made at a meeting of the Victorian Order of Nurses here in Ottawa on May 6, 1966, at 12 noon. The Minister of National Health and Welfare stated at that time in part:
One of the most important features of the Canada Assistance Plan is that it will make funds available for supplementary payments over and above payments made under such programs as old age security and the Canada Pension Plan. This will be particularly important during the early years of the contributory pension plan, when its benefits are building up.
Just in case the minister himself was not speaking with the authority of the government, I should like to quote again from the speech made in Fredericton, New Brunswick, on June 2, 1966 by the parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Westmorland. She said in part:
The basic aim of the Canada Assistance Plan is to close the gaps in the present programs. As a result, the federal government will share in payments higher than the present $75 a month limit in cases where more help is needed. And, needless to say, the assistance will be available in addition to the present $75 a month old age security pension.
And so I could go on.
We have all read in the papers recently, and the hon. member for Simcoe East referred to this, some interesting reports as to anxiety among Liberal members as to whether this kind of a program is going to meet the demands and the needs of our older people. I think the minister should have been at least frank and told us tonight what the government has in mind in this field.
I should like to say this again, and I hope I have made it clear, that we think where there are at the present time means test
Canada Assistance Plan programs it is a mark of progress to move to needs test programs, but in the field of assistance to our retired and older people where we now have two programs, namely th old age security program and the Canada Pension Plan, without any means test-plans under which people get their pensions as of right-I believe we would be doing our older people a disservice by bringing back any kind of test. We would be discriminating against those people as to the amount of pension they could get.
I know the line that is sometimes peddled, that any increase in pensions across the board will give extra money to people who do not need it; but I think this is one of the greatest pieces of fiction ever devised in this particular field. If I were a wealthy person I would know that the tax I have to pay during my working years, the tax I would have to pay as a retired person on my income as such and in social security taxes, the extra taxes I would have to pay on my old age security pension and the taxes I would have to pay because I was spending money on goods subject to sales tax, and the tax I would have to pay as corporation tax, would amount to more in the total package than what I would be getting back. Raising the pension for everyone does not amount to giving something to people who do not need it. They may get extra old age security money, but it is offset by taxes on income, sales taxes and as a result of the corporations tax structure now in existence.
We went into this whole question thoroughly during the meetings of that excellent committee on old age security in 1950, and I think we came up with a good plan. I think the Canada Pension Plan along with the old age security plan is good and that the combination of them will help the retired people of this country in the future, but I think this good picture and the good steps we have taken will be nullified and cancelled out if we now build into our old age retirement picture a means or needs test. Once we provide a plan which gives $10, $25 or $50 in assistance on a means test, then the pressure of that test will remain for a long time. Older people will only be able to meet their needs in that way and we shall be back where we were. There could even be pressure to reduce the $75 old age security pension on the basis that we could provide assistance in this other way.
I believe that the most important part of this whole Canada Assistance Plan, or the

June 14, 1966
Canada Assistance Plan whole problem it is supposed to deal with, was unfortunately only skated around by the minister, when he made the briefest allusion to it. He told us all about many other things but did not refer to this, and I hope before the debate on this question is over that some Liberals, like my good friend the hon. member for Brantford, will have something to say about it, along with some others on that side, which will cause the minister to realize that he cannot sell this piece of goods to the older people of this country.
The older people in Canada are aware of how close we came at the beginning of this session to passing a measure that would call for an increase in the old age security pension to $100 a month. They now wonder what happened, having got that close, to prevent our getting over the hump. I suggest that now is the time for this issue to be brought squarely out into the open; now is the time for the government to face up to the fact that we have to do something positive in this area.
I do not know why the minister skated around this issue tonight. Perhaps he did not have enough to eat and was too weak to cope with it. After all, he has had to sit here all day during one piece of legislation after another, and he has had little or no chance to go out and eat. Perhaps he was just ashamed of this program for our older people. I am sure there are others of his supporters sitting on that side of the house who are likewise ashamed, and I hope we will get a different view of this subject before the debate on this resolution concludes.
In spite of the sharp and critical things I have said about the failure of this legislation so far as the needs of our older people are concerned, I repeat that I welcome the progress being made in federal-provincial cooperation in the social welfare field. I welcome the idea of the federal government's moving into financial participation in these fields, but I hope that we will crown these things that are good with something really worthy of this parliament so far as our older people are concerned.

speechtext:
In order to wage a successful war on poverty several things must be done. The hon. member for Simcoe East was speaking about seeking out the pockets of poverty and then educating a member of the household so he could become a worth-while citizen. I think what we have to do in a war on poverty is educate the affluent society. I believe that the only way we can do this is by an honest approach on the part of all political parties.
Every shade of political opinion in this-house favours welfare legislation, and if we are to be honest with the electorate we cannot increase welfare action and reduce taxation. If the people of this country were to realize that from here on out all these programs will require additional taxation, I think there would be a greater chance to win. the war on poverty. Particularly in election campaigns or prior to election campaigns it has become the custom of governments to reduce taxation in order to entice the support of the electorate. I think that every political party from here on out that supports welfare legislation should be honest enough, not opportunist, to tell the public that it cannot reduce taxation.
I believe that the campaigns of welfare organizations such as the Red Feather campaigns do not solve the problem of poverty. I do not condemn them but I think they never solve the problem of poverty; they only postpone its solution. I think that welfare organizations such as Red Feather, and so on, ought to vacate the fields in which they are now engaged and let govermnent assume responsibility in these areas.
We have a system now in which we allow tax deductible philanthropy and it has arrived at the stage where in many cases the philanthropist seeks the advice of his accountant in order to determine how far his philanthropy can go. In this particular area it means that there are a lot of people who are able to support philanthropic endeavours, but do not do so, whereas if a program were provided from time to time, whether it be under an excess profits tax or whatever kind of taxation it might be, it would place everyone within the ambit of being a taxable contributor to the form of welfare programs upon which we are now embarked.
I think the question arises, where does prosperity end and where does inflation begin? An hon. member spoke about the depression in 1929. The United States of
June 14, 1966

America in trying to meet the problems that they faced in that era embarked upon what they called pump priming. Any sums of money that are going to be given under the headings mentioned in this resolution will be money that will be put back into the economy. Speaking particularly about the old age pensioner, or sums of money that he receives will be put back by him immediately into the economy.
I deal now with one other question, Mr. Chairman, namely that raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre who preceded me. He condemned the means test and said that the increase in the old age pension should be to $100 a month across the board without a means test. I would think that under this particular scheme it is not inconceivable that an old age pensioner, with the means test, will in certain instances be receiving more than $100 a month. If this be the case we would be making contributions to the old age pensioner who needs the money most.
If the increase is to $100 a month across the board, of course there will be people who will be receiving the extra $25 a month when they do not need it. But I think we at least ought to see how this legislation is going to work, because the old age pensioner who is now receiving $75 a month, and who in many instances has to supplement that pension by going to some welfare organization and receiving dole of some kind, will not be at all scandalized by going before a proper board, explaining his position and receiving in certain instances perhaps $125 a month. I believe that to attack this legislation on the basis of the arguments just made by the speaker who preceded me is to deny the very things that the hon. member seems to want to accomplish.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot agree with the closing remarks of the previous speaker, who is obviously making a case for the means test which the government is going
Canada Assistance Plan to use, even though they may call it a needs test. I believe, Mr. Chairman, that this proposal for co-ordinated plans is a reasonably wise one. I believe that the proliferation of plans that have existed until now might well be brought together and dealt with on an integrated basis. I think the minister put the case very clearly, and I wonder if he will allow me at this time to use the information that was made available to me. I believe that when this plan is approved it will be made retroactive. That is why I asked the minister what is the sum of money which will be spent in the current fiscal year, and whether it will include the money which will be paid retroactively.
It is obvious from the minister's explanation that this is to be a shared program. I believe that the provinces will be expected to contribute 50 per cent of the increased cost. I have some interesting observations to make in that regard.
May I also say at this time that many of the interested organizations across the country have lauded the logical integration of the plans in existence. I think it would be wise for the minister to set forth at this juncture a new and clearer definition in regard to disability pensions. This is one of the phases of our social program which seems to be applied from time to time on a discriminatory basis and, in many cases which I have personally seen, without good reason.

June 14, 1966
Canada Assistance Plan
It has also been indicated that the government is planning this scheme for a period of 10 years so as to allow for a phasing out during the transitional period before full payments are made under the Canada Pension Plan. So far as the older people are concerned, it is rather difficult to forecast their financial circumstances at a later time. At the end of the 10 year period our thinking in this field may well be completely changed if the status of our economy is not projected into the future. I do not think the minister should deceive us on the difference between a means test and a needs test, and I think the older people will agree.
We on this side of the house will not oppose this plan and we think that the sooner it is put into operation, the better. As I said previously, I appreciate the fact that the plan will be put into operation on a retroactive basis.
I was also interested in what the previous speaker has said in regard to additional taxation with reference to this and other plans in the future. I think if he were to examine the statistics regarding the present status of the old age security fund he would realize his error of judgment. I believe that the previous speaker was speaking in socialistic terms when he indicated that the government should take over all plans administered by the Red Feather and associated organizations and when he indicated he is not willing to allow anyone the right to do as he pleases with the money he has been able to earn. I think that his eyes would be opened if he realized the total cost in this regard.
Let us look at the existing figures. On page 5164 of Hansard of May 16, 1966 the following question which I put to the Minister of Finance appears:
What was the balance on account In the federal old age security fund as of December 31, 1965?
The Minister of Finance replied that the amount at that time was $139,974,933.15.
Yesterday I received a reply to a further question of mine which reads as follows:
What was the balance on account in the federal old age security fund for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1966?
The answer reads $216,982,834.44.
The next question which I asked the minister was:
What is the anticipated balance for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1967?

I received a fascinating answer relating the rate of growth of this fund. It amounts to $455 million.
On the basis of the figures given to us by the Minister of National Health and Welfare I think we should do our utmost to protect the way in which this particular fund is raised. I think we should be careful to consider this fund in the fight of what it will actually cost the government. It is very clear that over the years, at the rate specified by the minister, this fund might well take care of all charges under this scheme without additional taxation and even without additional contributions from other sources. I know the minister will disagree with me, but that might be so in the future. Such plans usually cost more than we bargain for initially, and therefore I do not believe that the provincial governments which will be dealing with the administrative disposition of this plan should be totally exempted from some responsibility. I think that the provinces will be so grateful to receive the benefits of such a scheme that they will offer to contribute to it if they have not already done so. The minister will know that much better than I. It is obvious to me that this plan will be of benefit to the recipients of this scheme without any additional increase in the income tax either now or later.
As I have said before, when my notice of motion was under discussion, and as I believe other hon. members have said in the past, I believe that a flat increase across the board should have been applied. Mr. Chairman, I wanted to say just a few words at this stage on the measure now before the committee, because of its importance to a great many of the people in this country. I want briefly to support the views of my colleague who spoke earlier and who argued against the provision in this resolution, or the bill to follow, which will in effect impose a means test upon the citizens of the country who are now in receipt of old age pensions. It is in my opinion a regrettable backward step that the minister proposes. It is one which we would not really have expected from him. The senior members of the house who, over the years, have fought the battle to remove the means test know that it was not an easy thing to do. We have read the debates and are aware of the
June 14, 1966

proposals put forward by my friends opposite that you must discriminate amongst these people, you must subject them to baring all their finances. These people will have to go through the degrading spectacle of opening up their personal affairs. Make no mistake about it, whether you call it a needs test or a means test, it is the same thing in the long run, no matter what the intention behind it is.
Let anyone go to the old age pensioners, as all of us in this house did during the election campaign, and ask them how they feel. It is all very well to get up in the house and talk sanctimoniously about old age pensioners as though they were a group of numbers, a group of a million or a million and a half people. You can say they are a group set apart, that we are not so much concerned with what they think, but this is what we are going to do. We are going to have a means test. We are going to go back to the old degrading attitude that prevailed many years ago. What you are going to end up with is an army of snoopers who are going to be commissioned to interview all these people. Whether you call it a needs test or a means test, it means individual investigation. You are not setting a standard basis at all. It means individual investigation of every old age pensioner to establish his need. This seems to be a retrograde step.
Perhaps before this debate ends, Mr. Chairman, we will have an opportunity of going into the final report of the special committee of the Senate on aging. I wish my friend opposite, if he has not already read it would read it. The report is a great tribute to the chairman of that committee, Senator Croll. The foreword to the report, and the report itself, adopts what I feel is probably the most humane and reasonable approach to the whole problem of aging in Canada. If the philosophy contained in this report were carried over into the legislation before us now, I think the measure would meet with a far greater response. This committee sat a great length of time, heard numerous witnesses and numerous briefs. One of its conclusions is set out on page 17 of the report. After investigating the whole problem of the old age pensioner and his needs, and the ways to meet these needs, the committee made this recommendation which is found on page 17 of the report:
Any suggestion that these older people, when the $75 pension is not sufficient, should be expected to depend for supplementation on public assistance after a needs test is utterly unacceptable.
Canada Assistance Plan
The committee made proposals to meet the problems of old age pensioners. I would not expect the government to announce right now their acceptance of the new concept of a guaranteed income program for these people. However, the one thing the committee did conclude after hearing these old age pensioners, associations and so on, after travelling all over the country, was that you must not supplement the $75 old age pension with any program based upon a needs test. In the view of the committee, this would be totally unacceptable. I would have thought this suggestion would have had some influence on the thinking of the government and the minister. Apparently it has not.
I want to make it clear, as I am sure other members will, that this is a retrograde step. The proposal is going to mean humiliation for pensioners. They are going to be individually investigated and asked to show all their affairs. All the degrading things that it took generations to do away with in this country are being reintroduced in one fell swoop. Who is introducing this? It is not the Conservative party, but the members of the Liberal party, the new, left Liberal party, the party of progress and leftism about which we have been reading in the newspapers. You are the people who are taking this retrograde step. I think it is most regrettable. We intend to fight it as strongly as we can.
There was one other aspect of this subject about which I wanted to make suggestions to the minister, Mr. Chairman. The Senate report makes it clear that you cannot ever really deal with the needs of our old age pensioners by dealing only with the amount of the pension you are going to give them. Even if we raised the pension to $100 a month tonight, as we would like to do, and even if that were acceptable to the government, we would not really be solving very much in the long run. Raising the pension is a relatively futile step unless you are prepared to deal with all the other things with which the pensioner has to deal in his daily life.
We have been asking, for example, for some program to deal with the rising cost of living in this country. If you go out and talk to old age pensioners, you will understand what they go through. You give them a $25 increase in pension and prices keep going up. Within a year this increase in the pension is lost and they have to come back and ask for more. If you are really going to help the old age pensioner, you have to do so by some sort

June 14, 1966
Canada Assistance Plan of integrated approach which will deal with the whole community in which he lives. One of the main things would be some action to try to deal with the high cost of living. This would be more advantageous, almost, than continuing to bump up the pension every time we have an election. This is the most important feature, and you hear it from every old age pensioner you meet.
Then there is the problem of the lack of proper housing for pensioners at rents they can afford. I am thinking for example of some countries in Europe where pensioners can rent accommodation for $5 or $6 a month. Here in Canada our pensioners are paying just whatever can be gouged out of them, except for the very few cases where we have any sort of low cost apartment units. If we were able to inaugurate proper housing proposals whereby old age pensioners could rent accommodation at low rates, this would be more useful than continuing to jack up the pension at every election.
If you are really going to help these old age pensioners, then another important matter is the payment for drugs and medical care. In my area we have old age pensioners who are paying more for drugs than they are for rent. They require a great many drugs, and the drugs are expensive. As I read the medicare proposal, it does not include drugs for pensioners. In any event this is another aspect of the problem with which we have to deal. As I have said, a mere increase in the monthly amount we give these people is not, in the long run, going to be that beneficial.

These are the main points I wanted to make. I want to re-emphasize again our absolute opposition to the retrograde aspect of the means test and the corps of snoopers it is going to create, because this is not the type of forward looking proposal that we would have looked for from the minister or the government. It is not a proposal that will meet with widespread support among the old age pensioners.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Canada Assistance Plan, as a statement of intent, will commend itself readily to members of the house and to all Canadians. At this stage it is simply a statement of intent, and until we see it becoming actually operative, in co-operation between the provinces and the federal government on a cost-sharing basis, we really cannot say that we have anything at all, because there is no directive on the part of

the federal government toward the provinces as to what they must do.
On the other hand this measure can be an exciting, revolutionary step, perhaps the most revolutionary among the whole group of public welfare acts, so that in this we are moving away from the concept of public welfare administered through a patchwork quilt of legislation covering different categories.
We shall have to define again need, and move away from the means test, as other speakers have said. It is of course true that the main question to be considered will be the benefits to Canadians as the result of this legislation.
We talk about the adequacy of intended benefits. I am sorry that I missed the first portion of the minister's statement, because I believe that he dealt to some degree with services to children. I am not clear whether the cost sharing features of the Canada Assistance Plan will be extended to children served by Children's Aid Societies. I raise this because one of the difficulties in the welfare structure is the inadequacy of the provision for children.
Child welfare agencies, whether they are
private or public agencies, or branches of welfare departments, are covering the services to children across the country. Those agencies are providing the rehabilitative services concerned with the basic unit in Canadian society, namely the family. I must point out that child welfare services have been understaffed all across the land. They lack the professional supervisory and administrative staff necessary for their operation, but they have still managed somehow to maintain a service, salving the public conscience in relation to child neglect.
It has become accepted that the program responsible for ensuring the provision of child welfare is a government responsibility. For this reason the exclusion of child welfare services from the Canada Assistance Plan is a very disturbing oversight.
I think that definitions which have been entered into are also very disturbing. You see, I do not think any other country in the world has introduced this kind of legislation where the "sky is the limit". One municipality or one province may decide that need within its area is minimal. For example, we all know that some people have said in the past that a washing machine for a family on welfare is a luxury, and not necessary. We have come a long way from then in our
June 14, 1966

definition of need. Similarly the attitude was that a refrigerator for some people might be considered a luxury; yet many of us have come to recognize a refrigerator, for some families, as an absolute need. In the same way a television set can be a very useful and needed item because it may help to keep the family together in the home. The definition of need becomes crucial in this legislation.
In recent years a good deal of attention has been given to the means test versus other approaches to the right to public assistance. The inference it is hoped would be drawn was that the means test procedure would automatically result in a proper benefit rate for recipients. I quarrel with that. I say that in many communities there is a quite different philosophy respecting the definition of need. The term is valid only, I say, if need is rationally defined and seen to include a number of requirements that are available outside the so-called welfare program. To be included in the definition of need should be the right to an adequate education, for example, and proper clothing, decent housing, and recreational facilities. All these factors, in my view, ought to be taken into account when defining need. Certainly we ought to think of more than marginal, bare existence when we define need. In short, all those things which contribute to the social usefulness of the citizen ought to be included in definitions of need if we are to make this an adequate program.
This is very unusual legislation because no standards are set. We may see great variations in programs across this country, where programs vary extensively between provinces because needs are differently defined.
If I understand the intent of the legislation correctly, it simply means that the federal government will share in the cost of the administration of these welfare services. Well, I can see that in some cases the provision of benefits will be much more generous than in others, because rather than the federal government's setting standards, or raising standards, this will not necessarily be done. This legislation adheres to a wide open door policy and does not seem to enforce on the provinces, or to suggest to the provinces, any similarities of standards that must be adhered to.
I am hopeful that the standards will be included in the legislation, when we see the act before us, or perhaps it can be done by regulation. Surely there must be minimum requirements for a province to live up to,
Canada Assistance Plan before it can benefit from cost sharing arrangements; otherwise this is the "sky is the limit" legislation. I am worried about that aspect of it.
The Canada Assistance Plan seems to suffer from the defect of assuming that the dollar figure to be applied to need is always rising, whereas the dollar figure to be applied to resources seems to be constant. Let me clarify what I mean. We see the position of pensioners-and many hon. members have spoken of the need of increasing the minimum pension to $100 a month. In the broad concept, need is defined in terms of constant dollar value, whereas the rest of the members of the community enjoy motorcars, washing machines, refrigerators, and an ever increasing standard of living. To the needy, some people say, "Doing without such things was good enough for my grandfather, therefore it must be good enough for you".
I believe in the concept that where members of the community live on an ever increasing standard, that those persons who are dependent on public assistance and on public programs of support should also be entitled to increasing needs. It is very discouraging, and detrimental to those persons who are left with fixed standards of living, to see other members of the community enjoying ever more affluent standards of living. I say that this whole concept must be carefully looked into, in order to make this a useful plan.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Another question that must be raised has to do with the adequacy of staff. Staff, not structure, will determine the adequacy of any legislation on this subject. However carefully legislation is formulated, if there is not adequate staff the families who are to be served will probably be more frustrated than ever and may even be harmed. For this reason I urge that every effort be made to increase opportunities for staff training. I find it difficult to express in strong enough terms my apprehensions regarding the manning of the welfare services, I draw attention to the need for large numbers of ancillary workers for the many responsible but comparatively uncomplicated tasks in welfare establishments. I agree that there should be excellent training programs to prepare workers for such tasks. I am a member of the social work profession and I have great sympathy for the tremendous needs of the profession itself. I agree we may not be using our resources adequately, and possibly are not finding ways of correctly

June 14. 1966
Canada Assistance Plan dividing our time between the more uncomplicated chores and those for which a higher degree of professional training is necessary. For these reasons I strongly urge the importance of a determined program of social work recruitment and education. In the absence of well qualified personnel, the availability of additional funds and ancillary personnel will create immediate confusion and may end in damage to the families concerned.
The organizations which are closest to families in want have always known that often families might have been strengthened and breakdown prevented had there been sufficient income, with assurance of its continuance for the duration of need and with administrative arrangements and methods which enable family members to maintain their self-respect. Family crises such as unemployment, or prolonged misfortune such as widowhood, would not then have had such power to destroy family happiness or have held so many threats to family unity. The Canada Assistance Plan, if utilized responsibly and generously across Canada, will mean a long stride toward goals which welfare agencies have coveted for Canadian families.
Mr. Chairman, that is the core of the remarks I intended to make at this stage. I look forward to seeing the legislation when it is finally introduced.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
I am pleased to support this legislation wholeheartedly. Nevertheless I hope it is a temporary measure. I take it that the purpose of this legislation-is to rehabilitate those whom it will assist-to enable them to earn a living and run the race we all run, without extra help.
I am not much in sympathy with those who say it does not matter how much help we give these people, that they will always be in the same place. The reactionaries who express this view would themselves be aghast at the suggestion that a physical cripple should run a race in competition with a perfectly healthy man. They do not realize that those who need the assistance to be provided by the measure we are considering are cripples, just as much as if they were physically crippled.
Nor can I accept the statement that Canada cannot afford such a program as this. We can certainly afford it. We are the wealthiest nation in the world-not the second wealthiest but the wealthiest. It was recorded in November last year that Canada is now the wealthiest nation in the world.

Yet with all our affluence there is still evidence of poverty of a kind which is a discredit to this nation. Only a couple of weeks ago I was reminded that in the town of Bancroft there are children who attend school without having eaten for two days; there are families where none of the children have shoes. I had a long talk with a lawyer in Bancroft and with a high school teacher there, and I verified the facts which they related to me-that half the energy of high school teachers there was spent in an attempt to feed and clothe their students. They buy clothes for them. One high school teacher, now retired, spent at least half his salary buying clothes for students so that they could go to get jobs. It does not matter how few these pockets of poverty are: As long as one family is in difficulty of this kind, it is a matter of great concern for this nation.
I am, as I said, very much in favour of this legislation, but I wish to express certain apprehensions in connection with the question of provincial co-operation. I realize that this program has to be administered provincially, and possibly locally; it cannot be done federally from Ottawa. I would remind the minister that there is a tendency in the smaller areas where the successful burghers of the town are usually elected to the council, to preserve the status quo and to save money

even though it may not be their own money-rather than spend it usefully on programs of the kind now envisaged. This legislation would be of no value if we do not succeed in rehabilitating most of the families who will be taking advantage of the legislation.
As the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa has pointed out, extensive training programs for social workers will be required. It is not enough for a social worker to be merely a distributor of money; he has to be trained to help a family back on its feet, an important and difficult job.
I read recently that a welfare worker could not handle more than 17 or 18 cases a year with any success. Obviously then we shall need a great number of trained workers in this field and the minister might well consider whether some of this money should not be spent on their training.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
Now I should like to say a word about assistance to older people who will come under this program. I hope that if they are to be included it will be only temporarily. I do
June 14. 1966

not believe that the pensioner thinks of himself, nor should we think of him, as a welfare case. He is not a welfare case. He is entitled to a pension as of right, the same as a veteran. The person now receiving the old age pension went through the depression years when normally he could have accumulated something to provide for his older years. He is now 65, 70 or 75 years old. He was the one who suffered and could not accumulate a nest egg during the depression.
Then the war followed the depression, and immediately after the war industry and business stratified their age limits so that when he expected to be employed profitably he found himself too old at age 45 or 50. Add to that the burden of educating his children much more expensively then he ever anticipated, and you will find he has a very good argument that he is a special case and is not a welfare case.
Therefore, as I suggested in my private members bill, I believe the old age pension should be merged with the Canada Pension Plan. The elderly person should be allowed to pay in a lump sum to that plan if he has the money, and if he has not got it he should be allowed to borrow it at a reasonable rate so that he may be enabled to join the plan. It is not his fault that the Canada Pension Plan was introduced when he was 70 years of age. This is the type of legislative change I would like to see.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not think it is necessary at the resolution stage to go into great detail regarding the proposed Canada Assistance Plan. We shall have ample opportunity to do that when the bill is before
Canada Assistance Plan us. I have followed the debate throughout the afternoon and evening and it seems most hon. members who spoke regard this measure as an attempt to fill gaps that have been left by already existent plans.
Canada has a fairly comprehensive program of welfare, and in terms of expenditure it has gone up rather astronomically in recent years. But, as pointed out by other hon. members, the postwar development was a rather hodge-podge if not confused approach to the total program.
The pattern of social welfare progress has
been similar in most western countries, with slow development up to the depression period, rapid development during the depression years and the war years, postwar adjustment and, more recently, as I have already mentioned, a certain air of uncertainty and confusion. The lack of specifics in this legislative proposal, the Canada Assistance Plan, would suggest that the government is going to endeavour to fill some of the awkward gaps not provided for in existing public schemes and voluntary programs.
Hon. members have issued a warning that it is going to be extremely difficult to standardize programs of this kind on a national basis. The hon. member for Portage-Neepawa, who is a professional in the field, has thoroughly covered problems with respect to the needs test. My hon. friends in the N.D.P. seem to take great exception to this phrase, a needs test, and are apparently equating it with a means test, which deals entirely with financial criteria. I would rather think in terms of the ideas that have been presented to us tonight by the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa, that the needs test is an attempt to deal with total needs, not only the financial and fiscal needs of the person requiring this sort of assistance but also the cultural, psychological and even the spiritual needs.
A person can be affluent so far as material goods are concerned, yet still be in need in terms of his total participation in society. I hope this is the definition and interpretation behind the proposals that will be placed before the house.
With respect to the matter of getting some sort of national co-ordination in social welfare programs, I would point out that in the initial stages it would appear that such programs were pioneered by provincial governments. Under the constitution they have responsibility for welfare, and some of the

June 14, 1966
Canada Assistance Plan earliest schemes, such as workmen's compensation, mothers allowances, and even old age pensions were initially brought forward by provincial authorities. In more recent times, due to the expanding idea and influence of the welfare state, the national government has moved more and more into the field of welfare.
I would direct the attention of the minister
to some excellent pioneering that has already taken place in the provincial sphere with reference to the proposal now before the committee. In 1959 the government of Manitoba passed an act known as the social allowances act which, so far as I can gather from the minister's introductory remarks, was designed to cover much the same area as the Canada Assistance Plan.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
I presume there has been a very close consultation with the provincial governments; but just to indicate how comprehensive the Manitoba legislation is, certainly as I read the act it is endeavouring to fill all the gaps and loopholes in existing welfare legislation. Perhaps I should draw to the attention of the minister the fact that section 3 of the social allowances act indicates that the purpose of the legislation is as follows:
Subject as herein provided, the government of Manitoba and each of the several municipalities in the province may take such measures as are necessary for the purpose of ensuring that no resident of Manitoba-
This is all comprehensive.
-including an Indian as defined in the Indian Act (Canada), lacks
(a) such things, goods, and services as are essential to his health and well-being, including food, clothing, shelter, and essential surgical, medical, optical, dental, and other remedial treatment, care, and attention;
Now, I think the minister will agree that is all-embracing and comprehensive. I presume this particular piece of legislation has been the pattern for the Canada social allowances act. Let me point out one or two gaps which have prevailed in existing legislation. One could refer in this conviction to wives deserted by husbands, a wife where the breadwinner has faced imprisonment, and the problems which arise where the breadwinner is institutionalized for a long period of time. I am just drawing examples from the Manitoba social allowances act, which covers all these important areas of social and welfare need.
If we are going to have a program which will be co-ordinated on a national basis and which will be reasonably standardized for

each of the provinces, as the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa pointed out it is going to require rather comprehensive study. We already have a shortage of trained personnel. The proposal has been made that there is a need to train ancillary personnel. This has been found necessary in the province of Manitoba, and such a program has been in operation under this legislation for the past six years. Both in the city of Winnipeg and the city of Brandon, for the past winter at least, there have been special training programs designed to meet the shortage of personnel. If you are going to operate a needs test in the broader concept you are going to require people who can train others to appraise and appreciate all the aspects of the social problem.
My final comment at this stage, Mr. Chairman, would be that I trust the government is not using this legislation as a substitute for the urgent necessity to increase the old age pension. A member of parliament gauges the needs of his constituents by the volume of correspondence he receives. Recently my correspondence has contained a growing number of letters from senior citizens who are faced with the financial pressure imposed by the rapidly rising high cost of living and who find they are being placed in a difficult financial position. Obviously there is a need for a basic pension of $100. I know the comment has been made that this problem will be resolved when the Canada Assistance Plan is implemented. I trust the minister has no such notion, and that as we proceed to approve this plan he will also take into consideration this immediate and pressing need of our senior citizens.
