speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am happy to have this opportunity to say a few words on the effects of the Canada Assistance Plan.
Involved in the bill now before us is a plan to share the cost of assistance between the federal government and the provinces. According to the minister, the cost of such program will amount to approximately $85 million.
In this case, improvements are sought in public assistance and welfare services for the unemployed, the disabled, the orphans, the needy mothers and other persons in need, in a word, to all the have-nots of the present system. The question is to help them by various means.
June 14, 1966

What are the means to help all these categories of outcasts of society? Are there any? The minister did not suggest many. He talks of improving this and that, but he has no practical solution. All those who have spoken following the minister have not suggested any practical solution to the problem either, it seems to me.
There is a tremendous social and economic problem to resolve and it relates to all areas of the economy; it is a problem that no one, until now, has been able to solve. It was partly solved by robbing those who were working to help those who were unemployed; by emptying the pockets of one who was working to give to an other who was out of a job, so that he could exist but not live.
At the present time, if you look at all the old people, all the old-age pensioners, all those who receive subsidies and if you listen to their requests and complaints, you will realize that they barely exist. Not one of them can say that he has enough. The cost of living keeps on increasing and all those pensioners, all those outcasts, are not getting any relief. The needs of those citizens have not been adjusted to the cost of living. In the case of children, we are asking that family allowances be increased because life is getting unbearable. People are living only by piling up debts. They live on credit, on money borrowed from finance companies.
The present economic system in Canada limits credit. It is no longer possible to live on borrowed money. The citizens are forced to pay back what they have borrowed already and they cannot borrow again.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
The situation is more serious than you think, Mr. Chairman. Reforms are needed in Canada, even in the field of production. Can one say that production is lacking in Canada? Are there citizens who are afraid that the land will not produce tomorrow? Are there members in this house who are afraid that the cow will not give milk tomorrow or that there will be a shortage of butter tomorrow morning in Canada? Not a single one. On the other hand, the people in general are not favoured by the system. They are afraid and worry about tomorrow. They are terribly afraid for tomorrow. They do not know if they will be able to get three meals tomorrow. That is serious, Mr. Chairman.
Why is there so much poverty in Canada when the land does not refuse to produce, when we have a production surplus? I read here in a newspaper that the Secretary of State for External Affairs stated in 1965, 1966,
Canada Assistance Plan 1967 we will give $75 million worth of food to various countries.
If we can help foreign countries, surely we can help Canadians in need. It is not money that Canadians want-you cannot eat dollar bills-it is production, something to feed the inner man. Nothing else. And if we have a surplus of products in Canada, why can we not manage our economic system, balance our economy so as to distribute this surplus? Why can we not take advantage of all the products with which our warehouses are bulging? Why can we not distribute them to meet everybody's needs? It is because our economy is topsy-turvy, unbalanced, and nothing has been done to correct that. Well, Mr. Chairman, the volume of money must be balanced with the volume of products. There must be as much money as there are products, and if we do that, business will run well, people will work and we will have what is necessary for our needy citizens. Production has surely been made to fill needs and not to be destroyed. It has not been made to let it deteriorate, it was meant to fill needs.
I ask the minister to assume his responsibilities in that regard. We must work towards meeting the needs in a country bursting with wealth, where we do not know what to do with our riches and our products. That is what we must do.
There are seven million producers in Canada; on the other hand, there are three million people who do not work half the time, who do not earn enough money to pay income tax. Something is wrong in the distribution system. We must look after that. We can surely make arrangements with the provinces but they have no money. The provinces cannot distribute the surplus of products in Canada. Well, if we would co-operate with the provinces, it would certainly be possible to find some solutions to the different economic problems with which we have to cope.
Those social problems are more serious than we think. Sad to say, a bomb was thrown in this parliament and others will follow, if we cannot settle the problem of daily bread, satisfactory housing at a proper rent in Canada. If we cannot do that, we will be destroyed and so will parliament. I wish I were wrong but I know I am not. Now for those reasons, it seems to me that we should pull ourselves together and see to it that this abundant and unfailing production is distributed in Canada. But we seem unable

June 14, 1966
Canada Assistance Plan to solve that problem and those who speak about it are laughed at.
Mr. Chairman, that problem should have been settled a long time ago in Canada. For a long time, those who have been suggesting solutions lay themselves open to ridicule. A day will come, Mr. Chairman, when they will be vindicated. I know that war settles many problems and indeed the Second World War has proved it, but I know that it also emptied warehouses and stores in Canada. Warehouses were bulging with goods when the war broke out in 1939. Well, there is still a surplus of goods now; yet, the war has been over for 20 years. Every year, we have a surplus production worth anywhere from $10, $12 to $16 billion. We had surpluses worth 16 billion in 1965-66. What shall we do with those surpluses, Mr. Chairman? Is the minister doing anything to try to distribute these goods, to meet the needs in Canada? Not much is done directly, but efforts are made to distribute scarcities, which is unusual. We eat according to the money we have, and dress, and house ourselves depending on our means-not according to our resources, our production-but according to the money we have. And the money we have in Canada is controlled by three or four financiers who make it terribly scare and prevent production from being distributed.
They prevent production from meeting the needs that exist.
Mr. Chairman, we certainly will not solve the problem by approving such abuses as exist in Canada.
Our democratic system, our capitalist system, is the best system in the world, but there are abuses and it is these that we must fight. We do not condemn the system at all, but we do condemn its main abuses. That is where we must work: to destroy the abuses within the system. We do not want socialism, nor communism; we want freedom, free enterprise, and that is what we must fight for, so that enterprise and men may be free, as God made them. We must work toward that goal, and men will be free to the extent where we can finance ourselves freely.
Finance is the reflection of all there is on earth. We cannot have a single potato without finance. Let the government take over the control of credit, of money, let it make sufficient credit to distribute the abundant production we have in Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I have many other things to say on unemployment, on production, on old

age pensions. Stinginess precludes increases in old age pensions; stinginess prevents money being made to produce. One member was saying a while ago that 70 per cent of our oldsters have only their old age pension to live on. When inflation is being felt in the country, when money is no longer worth anything, when the dollar is worth about 25 cents, how can one live?
How can you expect that demands will not be made for higher wages, higher pensions, higher everything? And when pensions, salaries, when everything is increased all over, this increases the costs of production. When the costs of production are increased, everything is increased. There is no way out. It is like a dog running after its own tail: there is no solution, Mr. Chairman, because it will never catch up with it.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, this problem has to be solved and I am asking the representatives of the people here in this house, to open their eyes and to look at things other than the old formulas of days gone by, formulas that are obsolete and inadequate and that must be made over. I ask them to open their eyes and to make over what needs to be made over. And whatever is going well, let it be. But what is going wrong must be corrected. The financial system is the only thing wrong with Canada. There is nothing wrong with production; there is an overabundance of products. If the government were to put to work all the unemployed, all those receiving social welfare allowances, all those who could work but are not working because they cannot be forced to under our system, how much would the country produce? Canadian production could be trebled if our physical forces were put to work.
Mr. Chairman, this cannot be done at the present time, but it could be done if we opened our eyes instead of keeping a diabolical system under which our people are starving in the midst of plenty.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks on the resolution before us and speak specifically to two, or perhaps three, points. I should like to say that I agree in great part with the remarks of the hon. member for York East, particularly with his statements about the use of these funds for rehabilitation. I must say that when I read the resolution on the order paper I was concerned about the repetitive references to providing assistance for welfare services and
June 14, 19S6

welfare service programs. I sincerely hope- and in this connection I echo the sentiments of the hon. member for York East-that the idea will be to provide rehabilitation if at all possible as the prime concern of this proposed plan, because I think it is so much more important to human dignity to give people the opportunity to fend for themselves and to provide for themselves. This surely should be paramount, and we should not be concerned with just handouts to help, perhaps for political reasons, meanwhile paying only lipservice to the needs of so many people across Canada.
I do not speak lightly when I talk about lipservice in this measure, because we have heard a great deal from many members of this house-and I agree with them-about the old age pension and the need to raise the amount to $100 a month. Surely it has become evident, not only in this house but across the country, that there is an immediate need for such a program to be carried out. Surely the number of letters we are all receiving and the number of interviews we have had with the old folk have made us realize the fantastic numbers of these people across the country who do not have sufficient to keep body and soul together.
In answer to a question put by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce, I believe the minister stated that the moneys to be appropriated in 1966-67 for this plan would be $85 million.
I will leave that aspect of the matter for a moment. I listened to the hon. member for Cartier, and I must say I have heard similar observations from the Prime Minister as well as the minister, when he put forward the argument that the government cannot increase the old age pension across the board because it will cost somewhere in the neighbourhood of $800 million. They say that we cannot afford it. I heard the hon. member for Cartier make the statement that the means test, or the needs test, whatever you want to call it-I do not think we should deal in semantics this evening-would be very beneficial to some because through the Canada Assistance Plan those who really need assistance may receive $125 a month instead of $100, or perhaps $150 if there is real need present. But let us look at this statement, in view of the amount the minister said would be required to increase the old age pension, namely $800 million. This matter has not been raised by myself but was raised by the Prime Minister and members on the other side of the house.
Canada Assistance Plan
If we look at the Senate report on the aging I think it is said quite clearly-I do not have the report with me but I am sure we could clarify this point at any time-that 15 per cent of those in receipt of old age pension are actively needing and receiving welfare service, social aid or whatever you want to call it. If you take 15 per cent of $800 million-and I believe the figure is actually more than that, but I will use the figure of $800 million to allow for my poor mathematical progress-you come up with a figure of $125 million. In other words, to raise to just $100 the old age pension of the 15 per cent who are in need now and are already receiving welfare service will cost $125 million, and the Canada Assistance Plan provides only $85 million.
What sort of legerdemain is this, that we can try to fool the people that we will give them $125 a month or $150? Surely this sort of thing is absolute nonsense. Surely the need is there, that we must now provide for the old age pensioners who need assistance, and we must provide adequately across the board for them as has been said so many times this evening.
I would ask the minister to heed the remarks of the hon. member for Cartier-and I am sorry he is not in the chamber-a member of his own party, who said that we should not be afraid to tell people that it is going to cost them money. I agree that we should not be afraid to tell them when we have to raise taxes, perhaps, in order to provide for these elderly people in Canada who are so desperately in need today. I agree with the hon. member for Danforth when he refers to the increase in the old age pension as being only part of this problem. Certainly integration of such things as the provision of adequate housing for the aged is important. This is clearly laid out in the Senate report on the aging.
It came as a great surprise to me to find that, despite the assertions of the Minister of Labour with regard to the tight money policy that there would still be money available through C.M.H.C. for the provision of homes for the elderly, nowhere in the National Housing Act is there any reference at all to homes for the elderly-none whatsoever. There is only reference to low cost rental housing on the basis of economics. There is nothing to take care of the elderly, as has been suggested in the Senate report on the aging.
To come back to the question of rehabilitation for a moment, Mr. Chairman, I wonder

Canada Assistance Plan whether, when we see in the resolution the words "specialized projects for assisting and rehabilitating persons in need or likely to become persons in need", this will be extended-I sincerely hope it will-by the minister and the government to old age pensioners and others, such as the chronically ill. I refer to the facilities for rehabilitation through physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and so on, in our nursing homes.
Surely there must be integration in this respect with the nursing homes. We need more nursing homes. I ask the minister, how much money will be provided for such things as increased home care, which has been recommended so many times across this country? I do not see anything in the resolution to indicate that such a provision will be included in the program. I believe these are extremely important matters to which the government should direct their attention and pay heed to the desires and wishes of groups which have already approached the government and presented briefs pleading that they do something along this line.
I congratulate the minister on one thing, namely the inclusion in the program of assistance for the rehabilitation of the mentally retarded. This is a matter that the Canadian Association for Retarded Children has for many years been advocating to the government in briefs and every other possible method. I believe it is extremely important that we do something to increase the rehabilitation of the mentally retarded, particularly those who do not fall under the educational acts of the provinces, are not considered educable and therefore are not included in the educational programs of those provinces.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
I did wonder, however, with all the amendments to the various acts in this resolution, about the omission of one. Perhaps some time toward the end of this discussion the minister could comment on it. On February 21 of this year I asked a question of the ministry. It appears at page 1499 of Hansard and as follows:
Does the government plan to introduce legislation this session to provide capital and operational assistance to sheltered workshops for the mentally handicapped throughout Canada?
The answer was:
Operational assistance is already being provided to a number of sheltered workshops for the mentally handicapped under the federal provincial vocational rehabilitation and vocational training programs.

Of course we are all well aware of this. However, I wonder whether the act will contain amendments governing vocational rehabilitation to allow for the improvement of those of the mentally retarded who could be trained to work in industry in sheltered conditions. It seems to me that it would be well worth the government's time to look into this matter. I do not care what makes a person handicapped, whether he is paraplegic, mentally retarded or blind; the important thing is the rehabilitation, and the keynote of this matter is that they are handicapped.
As the minister may know, there is at present a crusade for Canada's mentally retarded. The organizers of this crusade plan to raise over the next five years $15 million by public subscription to take care of several programs that have been set up. There are 13 such projects across Canada. I will mention one in the rehabilitation sphere which is taking place in Edmonton, Alberta, for the training to independence through the application of the latest industrial technology, which demonstrates that the retarded can work on a competitive basis although in sheltered conditions.
In his remarks the minister made reference to the fact that he will provide aid for these types of projects. Was he suggesting that he will help this particular crusade through the Canada Assistance Plan? This year this crusade will require $5 million and it is estimated that it will require $15 million over the next five years.
If such is the minister's intention, then I think those people across Canada who are vitally concerned with this problem will be most pleased to hear this from him. I might point out that the lives of over two million Canadians, which is a greater number than those inhabiting some of Canada's largest cities, are directly affected, being members of families who have someone stricken by retardation. This is not a small matter. Surveys have shown that special care for the retarded by institutions, agencies and families costs close to $100 million a year, enough to build the monument to the Minister of National Defence to which reference has been made in the last few days.
I wonder if there is enough in the $85 million that is being suggested to provide the kind of help that is so vitally needed. I would just like to point out that the Canadian Association for Retarded Children has shown that by carrying out these projects and other similar projects for the mentally retarded,

Canada's economic health can be improved in several ways. May I list them briefly. The program helps to improve Canada's economic health in the following ways:
By integrating necessary services for the retarded with regular health, welfare and educational resources;
By continuing and extending methods for cutting down costs of long-term institutional care;
By transforming more tax consumer retardates into self-sufficient members of the community;
By moving toward maximum efficiency in development of the nation's manpower;
Commercial and industrial interests are improved in the following ways:

By adding new people to the ranks of the gainfully employable;
By making new techniques of training and rehabilitation available to commerce and industry for application among normal workers.
Let me say in summary, Mr. Chairman, that when we discussed the health resources fund I echoed the statement that it was too little and too late. Now I would like to say about this plan that perhaps it is not too late, but it is certainly too little.
The minister said that the government would attempt through the Canada Assistance Plan to provide at least a comparable amount to the sum contributed by the provinces to some of the assistance programs. May I point out to the minister that in the province of Saskatchewan old age pensioners receive through old age assistance an average of $2.50 a month over and above their $75 a month. I wonder what they will think when they hear that perhaps the government will give them $5 instead of $2.50 a month. Is this enough? I think a clear answer has been given by many speakers. It is far too little, and something must be done to increase the aid to our old age pensioners. This is something which should be done as quickly as possible, not some indefinite tomorrow or next week. Assistance is needed to lift these people out of the degradation in which we, the parliament of Canada, have allowed them to stay. We must do something to lift them to the level of decency that they most certainly deserve as pioneers in this great country of ours.

Mr. Chairman, I would not want to delay the house very long, but I would make a few remarks in connection with the legislation under consideration. Having taken a careful look at the resolution before us, we cannot but support it, at least in principle. It is a brilliant statement of intentions, but it will surely be necessary to wait for the details of this legislation before deciding whether it is actually worth as much as the minister wants to make us believe.
Looking at this legislation, Mr. Chairman, one gets the impression that the government would want to settle all the problems of the needy at once, but we may entertain doubts about that, since we have striking examples of the lack of foresight or of the lack of enthusiasm in meeting the needs of the destitute.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
For instance, I would simply point out the refusal of the government to accept our proposal to raise old age security pensions to $100 per month. Mr. Chairman, if there is one group in our society which surely deserves our gratitude and our financial support, it is the state pensioners.
I agree that we should improve the plight of the needy, but we must go further. There are numerous other sectors of society which

June 14, 1966
Canada Assistance Plan must be assisted. The program put forward is explicit and alsp refers to a great number of measures which are shared cost programs, under provincial and federal jurisdictions. In fact that will give rise to several problems, and I have no doubts that, while exercising his rights, the minister will not want to infringe upon the rights of the other parties to those programs.
Mr. Chairman, I do not think I am mistaken in saying that this measure is part of the big war, in words rather than deeds, against poverty. Apparently, as soon as this government intends to take steps to reduce poverty, poverty increases in Canada. This is no doubt due to the increasingly high cost of living and the constant danger of inflation which threatens all of us from day to day.
Well, it seems that in both fields, that is the high cost of living and inflation, the government could take steps to wage a real war against poverty and win the admiration of the people. The population is fed up with promises that the situation will improve; they want to see the government take action. As I do not want to take up any more of the time of the house and in order to afford the government the opportunity to implement its various programs, I will say no more, and await the introduction of the bill, reserving the right to criticize it if need be.

speechtext:
I was not going to speak tonight on this resolution, and in view of the minister's remarks I shall only take a few minutes, so perhaps his wishes will be fulfilled. I was provoked into speaking on this resolution for three reasons. The first one is the multitude of speeches on the problem that
IMr. Ricard.l
I have heard and the fact that there have been few voices from the east. This subject is of concern in the east because of the age groups there, to say nothing of the political implications as a result of the last election on November 8.
Another reason that I have been provoked into saying a few words lies in the two fundamental faults which I submit are contained in this resolution. I am not like the hon. member for Yorkton, who was going to use buckshot but decided there was no point in firing. I say you can use two broadside attacks on this plan, as it is presently drawn.
Then, Mr. Chairman, I am somewhat surprised at the minister from my own province, who is well known for his liberal tendencies not only politically but in social welfare programs, advocating and sponsoring such a resolution which perpetuates the means test on two levels. First, I should like to discuss the means test at the dominion-provincial level. As I understood the minister's opening remarks, the purpose of the bill which is to follow this resolution is that the federal government will contribute to the provinces on the basis of what those provinces can pay. I submit that if this is the intent of the measure then, instead of this legislation unifying Canada in the fashion of the concert of voices on the government side either on a one nation or two nation basis, this measure is going to divide Canada into ten different provincial areas. It will do so on the basis that one province can pay so much and another province can pay so much; the various provinces have different abilities to pay. I submit that whether you call it a means test or a needs test, you are driving a wedge between provinces rather than unifying the provinces under this particular program which, potentially, is a unifying program.
I submit on that ground alone, this resolution should be amended at the bill stage so that assistance is given to the provinces without discrimination on the basis of the ability of those provinces to pay for assistance in the way indicated in the resolution. Whether you call it a means test or a needs test, you are merely getting into a debate on a psychological distinction in semantics. I submit that whether or not the minister or the government like the words "means test", they cannot find solace in the confusion of trying to interpret needs or means. You will define means by defining needs, and vice-versa. You
June 14. 1966

cannot change the thing by calling it a different name; you cannot change a goose to a gander or a goose to a chicken, merely by a change in name.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
I have mentioned two reasons for my disagreement with this resolution. The first is that it is going to perpetuate the differences between the provinces. We have a minister sitting here on the government side tonight who claimed he was going to integrate the services. This plan has a potential for helping to integrate assistance to all the provinces. Yet, by having different levels of payments based on the ability of the provinces to pay you will have disintegration. You will have old age pensioners and people like that in Saskatchewan, Ontario or British Columbia wondering perhaps whether if they had been born under any other star, or in any other province, their benefits which would be based on the province's ability to pay might not have been somewhat different.
The minister of course is familiar with the legislation the government has brought down. His views are exemplified in the measures providing for assistance in education, which were commendable, and in the health resources program which he manoeuvred through the house today or yesterday. There is an adjustment in those measures with respect to certain parts of the country which have not the ability to pay as much as other parts.
In this legislation there is no such adjustment. The fact is that the inability of some provinces to pay will be perpetuated, and you will have not one nation, or even two nations, of which people have been talking for some time, but ten nations, each one of which would have different levels of assistance.
Because of that, and the fact that there is a means test-and hon. members will remember all the things which have been said about the means test-I am surprised at the minister. He deserves much credit for much of the recent legislation he has piloted through the house, but he is to be somewhat reprimanded, in my view, for trying to pilot this resolution through the house, a resolution running counter to most fundamental welfare programs that the present government and the past government brought in.
As far as assistance is concerned, Mr. Chairman, you do not have assistance. This legislation should try to stimulate a person, rather than stagnating his personality. If you are going to have handouts, with means tests
Canada Assistance Plan and all that that means, you are going to stagnate personalities. We have heard members speaking of the need to help, rather than to give handouts. For these reasons I must register a strong protest against the resolution as it presently stands. I hope that in the bill stage some of the major defects that you could hit with a broadside might be rectified so that the bill could sail through, and be the kind of bill to fulfil the minister's wishes, and satisfy the urgent needs of many Canadians.

maintopic: HOUSING-REQUEST FOR C.M.H.C. FINANCING FOR OLDER BUILDINGS
HOUSING-REQUEST FOR C.M.H.C. FINANCING FOR OLDER BUILDINGS
speechtext:
On June 1, I addressed a question to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) in his capacity as the minister answering for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I asked when we could expect legislation implementing the government's election promise that National Housing Act financing would be extended to older homes.
In reply, the minister said:
I do not recall any such election promise, but I can assume that when government policy in this matter has been settled, it will be announced in this house.
I thought that for the record I might refresh the minister's memory. I have in my possession a document called "The Policies of the Liberal Party". This was put out in 1963 and on the opening page it stated:
These are the policies of the Liberal party of Canada. The purpose of this document is to give the voters of Canada a clear statement of what they will be doing if they entrust the country's affairs to a new Liberal government.


A great deal of self-congratulatory comment follows. Later on the document says:
The proposals that the Liberal party puts before you are not election promises, cooked up for the occasion to attract support from this group and that. They are nation-wide policies developed during five years of careful study and intensive discussion among Liberals all over the country.
Then the document says: "We put these policies forward for the next four years."
In another section, dealing with community services and housing, there is a paragraph which promises toextend national housing legislation to provide insured mortgages for the purchase of existing homes as well as for building new homes.
I took that to mean that this is the Liberal party policy, and I think it is a good one. It is one for which we have been asking for several sessions. It works a hardship on young people if they must move to the suburbs to take advantage of C.M.H.C. financing provisions.
For several years I have asked when the government would be prepared to present this legislation to us. The only reason I raise the matter tonight is because of the minister's answer that he did not recall any such election promise. But from our experience with this government we all know its propensity for honouring its commitments. We heard much talk about that on previous occasions, and knowing the views of the government in that regard I wanted to draw this election promise to the attention of the minister.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
I am sorry that I have had to keep the minister in the house so late tonight, after his arduous efforts on the labour front, but it only enforces our argument that we should have two ministers, one to look after labour and the other to be in charge of housing and who could answer questions of this type. Now that I have refreshed the minister's memory on this election promise, I ask him when these commitments will be honoured?

However, I do recall the commitment that was made in 1963 and I can assure the house that in the short time that intervened between the election of 1963 and election of 1965, the government went a long way to implement the promise which was contained in the 1963 election platform to which the hon. member has referred.
I am sure he will recall the symposium that was held in Toronto when the amendments made in 1964 to the National Housing Act were discussed at length. It was a very useful exercise and one that I am sure will have beneficial results. On that occasion reference was made to the point raised by the hon. member tonight.
It was then pointed out that in the amendments which I introduced to the act in 1964 we had made a first and important step toward implementing the promise that we gave in 1963. We included in our new urban renewal program provision for loans to embrace houses that were included in any urban renewal area. It was explained at that conference, and at others which were held across Canada, that this was but the initial step, and those 11 conferences were important for the ideas that were raised at them by municipalities and others all across the country.
After the first symposium I was not surprised that at almost every one of these conferences a suggestion was advanced to the effect, "Well, now that you have made your experimental run, will you give consideration to extending or amending the National Housing Act to include loans for the repair or for the modernization of existing houses"? Quite frankly I doubt if at any of these conferences any problem received more attention than the one mentioned by the hon. member.
I am not making any commitments because the government policy has not been decided, but I can assure you that when amendments to the National Housing Act are introduced, I hope later this year-and this is included in the government's legislative program-provision may be made to take care of the situation which has been raised by the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott).

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday June 8 I asked the following

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion question of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen):
Is the government still giving consideration to increasing the old age pension?
I asked this question on the eve of the bringing before the House of Commons by the government of the resolution in connection with the Canada Assistance Plan. Tonight this resolution has been brought forward. The resolution proposes legislation to establish a program for sharing with the provinces the cost of assistance to persons in need. Among those mentioned in the resolution as being in need are the older persons, as well as mothers of children, disabled persons and the unemployed. A provision is forecast providing amendments to the Old Age Assistance Act, among other acts.
My question is asked because I, as a member of parliament, believe that benefits to old age pensioners and senior citizens should be benefits which will accrue to such persons as of right rather than of need.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: OLD AGE SECURITY-CONSIDERATION OF INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PENSION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: OLD AGE SECURITY-CONSIDERATION OF INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PENSION
speechtext:
The Old Age Assistance Act, as presently administered in Ontario and other provinces, is antiquated. The means test as provided in these provinces is not an up to date provision for the health and welfare of older citizens.
A year or two ago I endeavoured to obtain assistance for a man between 65 and 70 years of age who no longer, because of his physical condition, was able to earn a proper livelihood. His wife was employed part time at a household in Brantford and her annual income was not quite $1,000 a year. At her age she could not work for longer hours or more days than she did. They owned their own home. When their assets, including a small bank account and their house, as well as his meager income and her meager income were added up, this gentleman could not qualify for assistance. They were told to spend what they had in the bank and then this man could re-apply. It was a shocking thing to me that this person could not qualify. Since that time I have not thought much of the means test under the Old Age Assistance Act. I told him never to dispose of their home, no matter what they did.
There are older persons, without even a home of their own, living in old attics in Brantford and paying high rents, whose only income is $75 a month under the old age pension. I want to see an end to this situation
June 14, 1966

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion which exists in Canada; I want to see an end to the idea ot a means test for old age pensioners in Canada who desire more income than the present old age pension. I should like to see Canadian citizens who no longer can earn an income, because of age, be able to live in dignity in their retirement. Therefore, I want to see an increase in the old age pension and I want senior citizens to be removed from the class of welfare cases once and for all. I am far from sure that the implementation of the Canada Assistance Plan will have this effect, particularly from what I have heard in the debate tonight.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
In the Ottawa Citizen of today, Tuesday, June 14, there appears an editorial from which I should like to quote. The Ottawa Citizen has always been very close to the government, and this editorial adds to the rumour that something additional might be done for the benefit of old age pensioners. The editorial states in part:
There are reports that the Pearson government is considering special action to assist elderly persons who stand to get little or no benefit from the Canada Pension Plan. The idea would be to supplement by up to $25 a month the present $75 old-age security pension.
Perhaps the stage has been reached where such a move is required.
Then after referring to a surplus of $240 million in the fiscal year ending March 31 in receipts under the old age security fund the editorial states:
If the federal government decides to supplement the old-age security pension, and if the economy does not grow sufficiently to make this possible under the present arrangement, then it should raise the contribution rate under the special formula.
I should therefore like to hear from the minister as to what is being considered by the government to alleviate the income problems of all persons 65 years of age or more, and to provide a remedy for all those persons who will never be able to obtain benefits under the Canada Pension Plan because of their age and the date when they were born.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
maintopic: OLD AGE SECURITY-CONSIDERATION OF INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PENSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just a few evenings ago, in connection with a similar question, I pointed out that in the current fiscal year, 1966-67, federal expenditures in respect of old age security will amount to $1,035 million. It should be pointed out also

that in 1963-64 the federal government was spending $755 million on old age security payments. Thus in a period of three years outlays have been increased by $280 million, or 37 per cent. During this period of three years the level or rate of benefit has been raised and the number of persons covered has been increased by 100,000 through lowering the age to 69.
I want to say that more should be done, and I am sure that more will be done to improve the lot of our old age security pensioners; but I also want to point out that the record over the past three years in this field has been one of achievement. We have in effect today a substantially more generous and much broader program in support of old age security recipients than was in effect when this government took office three years ago.
These improvements have not been confined only to old age security. A steadily increasing level of retirement benefit will be payable under the Canada Pension Plan commencing next January. The lowering of the age under old age security to 68 in January will also extend protection to another 100,000 persons heretofore not covered.
The medicare registration, which will soon be before this house, will be especially important to older people in Canada. The incidence and duration of illness is greater in older people. With the combined benefits of hospital and medical care our older people will have a greater sense of security, knowing that these health needs will be met. Along with this there will be provision under the Canada Assistance Plan for other health care services such as drugs, nursing services and prosthetic appliances, and for income supplementation for those whose budgetary requirements are insufficient.
These are but a few of the things the government is doing or has done for Canada's senior citizens. I want to express my personal appreciation to the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Brown) who has maintained a keen and humanitarian interest in this question of providing income support for Canada's older citizens. That interest is shared by the government of Canada and will be demonstrated as we develop further programs of support for Canada's older citizens.

NORTHERN AFFAIRS-CONSTRUCTION OF REPLICA OF "GRANDE HERMINE" FOR EXPO '67
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must first of all apologize to those members who are still in the house for having to listen to me come back to the question of the Grande Hermine. However, I wish to state to the parliamentary secretary who is here tonight that I intend coming back to this question as long as it is necessary. I will insist on raising the question until justice is done to history, and there is by the government an acknowledgement of the historical events of this country, and they are placed in their proper order.
I think it would be very illogical if we thought of celebrating our centennial year in 2049 because Newfoundland joined confederation in 1949, rather than having it in 1967 to commemorate the beginning of confederation.
I am sure we would not have done this after the western provinces, British Columbia, New Brunswick or Prince Edward Island came into confederation, but rather would have celebrated our centennial from the signing of the British North America Act, which was its beginning. Next year is the time to celebrate our centennial, namely 1967. However, in this case we seem to want to celebrate the second voyage of Cartier to Canada. We have forgotten that he came here a first time.
The other night after the parliamentary secretary listened to my plea, all I got from him was a prepared statement which was an exact replica of the announcement made by the minister on March 18. There was no rebuttal but simply a statement. I think we can expect more than this from the department. There must be reasons for their action in this regard and I believe those reasons should be made known to those of us who have spent many years working on this project and have now seen it, as I have said, taken over or expropriated by the department, without any consultation with those who first thought of the idea.
All I received at that time was a weak, defenceless and worthless reason to justify the actions of the government. No mention was made of the work accomplished over a period of four years. There was no mention of the worth based on the value of this project, its place in our history and the economic values which develop from its exploitation.

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion What is happening now, as I said the other night, is that we have planned to do something that will cost this country much more money. The decision was made without the proper studies being first of all carried out. We are now faced with the problem of having to dismantle this ship after it has been built and after spending many, many thousands of dollars to get it under two single bridges and one double bridge. The next thing that arises is that we discover the bed of the St. Charles river is federal property and that the province is asking that it be ceded over to them in order to develop the Cartier-Brebeuf park. I think these things are serious and the government should not proceed with its plan until all the studies are completed. In my opinion these studies will definitely prove that it is not rational in any way whatsoever to proceed with placing this ship in the Cartier-Brebeuf park.
[DOT] (10:30 p.m.)
It is only recently that the city of Quebec has asked the federal government to return to it the scale model belonging to the city of Quebec as constructed by surveyor Duberger in 1806. This model now rests in the Daly building here in Ottawa, and anyone who wishes to see what the city of Quebec looked like in 1806 must make a trip to Ottawa and take a photograph of this model. I do not know what this adds to Ottawa, but if this city insists on being the proprietor of the model, why should it not at least loan this scale model to the city of Quebec so that they also can have their memento of 1806? I think Quebec has the right to demand it, and if Ottawa lends them the model then Quebec might not insist on our ship being berthed there permanently.
For this reason and also because we have made a statement that we intend to proceed with these plans, it is evident that no study whatsoever has been made and that there is only one logical place where this ship should be berthed permanently, and that is in the birthplace of Canada. I think that the department should at least give some consideration to this request and, as I have already stated, ask representatives of the national Historic Sites and Monuments Board to appear before the standing committee so that we will have a chance to question them and try to justify our claim.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources

I wish to assure the hon.
June 14, 1966

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion member for Gaspe (Mr. Keays) that I appreciate the interest he is showing in the history of Canada and to remind him that in 1934 the Historic Sites and Monuments Board caused a cross to be erected in Gaspe where in 1534 Jacques Cartier landed.
I also understand his concern in view of the many representations that have been made to him from his constituents to retain locally as much as possible the association of Jacques Cartier with the Gaspe region. However, I would like to take this opportunity to reassure him that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) has given the representations of the hon. member and those of his constituents very serious consideration. In so doing he was also guided by the Historic Sites and Monuments Board advisory committee which advises him
on the historical importance of events that have occurred in Canada.
In considering the site where the Grande Hermine should be located after Expo '67 we should recall that the Grande Hermine was not part of Cartier's fleet at the time of his landing in Gaspe in 1534. I am informed that the Grande Hermine was only used in 1535 when it took Cartier to the junction of the St. Charles and Loiret rivers where he spent eight months, including an eventful winter.
The site where Cartier wintered is the area where the Cartier-Brebeuf National Historic Park is being developed. According to the present plan, I understand that the Grande Hermine will be relocated in this park after Expo '67 and it is there that it will be displayed as a prominent feature.
